Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	I wish
to invite the attention of the government to a matter of great importance and urgency to the people residing in the county which I represent. Up to a few days ago, the village of Ste. Emelie de 1'Energie stood proudly like a sentinel at the foot of the Laurentian mountains. A week ago to-day, at exactly this hour, this thriving village, in the constituency which I have the honour to represent was destroyed by fire. It is estimated that

about 85 per cent of the village has been so destroyed. The parish church, the convent and some 75 dwellings have been reduced to ashes. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DESTRUCTION OF THE VILLAGE OF STE. EMELIE DE L'ENERGIE
speechtext: I can only say that the government will consider very carefully, and I am sure as sympathetically as may in the circumstances be possible, the statement my hon. friend has made. In cases where conflagrations have destroyed towns or villages I think the federal government has given as a general rule such assistance as it could on application in the first instance by the government of the province in which the municipality affected was situated. Occasions have arisen where the government was in a position to render something in the way of special aid, as for example, co-operation with the Red Cross in the loan of blankets, tents and the like. I think the government has always responded quickly where a request for such has been made. Beyond that, where the request resolves itself into a matter of financial assistance, it would be impossible to say what action the government might find it possible to take until after the province concerned has acted in the matter, and we know what it is doing.

Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou) (Minister of National Defence) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the provisions of the Militia Act, chapter forty-one of the Revised Statutes, 1906, relating to calling out the active militia in aid of the civil power, and to provide,-
1.	That the attorney general of a province upon receiving notification from a judge of a superior or county or district court, having jurisdiction in the place concerned, that the services of the active militia are required in aid of the civil power, may, upon being satisfied that the services of the active militia are so required, make a requisition whereby the district officer commanding is required to call out the active militia, or such portion thereof as he considers necessary, for the purpose of suppressing or preventing any actual or anticipated riot or disturbance.
2.	That such requisition shall contain an unconditional undertaking that the province shall pay to His Majesty

Militia Act Amendment
all expenses and costs incurred by His Majesty in calling out the militia as aforesaid.
3.	That in every case the attorney general who made the requisition shall within seven days thereafter cause an inquiry to be made into all the circumstances and send a report thereof to the Secretary of State.
4.	That all expenses incurred by His Majesty in so calling out the militia in aid of the civil power shall be paid to His Majesty by the province of which the attorney general made the requisition, and His Majesty may retain from any annual grant payable by Canada to such province and under the control of the parliament of Canada, any unpaid balance of moneys due to His Majesty by such province under this provision.
5.	That the expenses and costs occasioned by the calling out of the militia shall, pending payment by the province, be advanced in the first instance out of the consolidated revenue fund by the authority of the Governor in Council, but shall be payable by and recoverable from the province to and by His Majesty as moneys paid by the latter to and for the use of the province at the request of the latter.

That act was amended in certain details in 1873, again in 1877, and again in 1883.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to make myself heard if the House will only listen. The trouble was that the House was not listening. The year 1883 marked the last act which provided for bringing out the military without the intervention of a judge. The right to call out the military in those early days was vested in the hands of an official whom nobody ever heard of today, the custos of a county, or the warden of a county, or the mayor, as the case might be. Again in 1904 the act was (further amended, and we have been working practically under the provisions of the 1904 act during the last twenty years. Apart from (details, it provided that if in towns or cities a difficulty arose, die mayor or warden of the town or municipality, or if they refused or were unable to act, then a county or district judge, and in unorganized districts where there was no mayor or warden, the district judge or superior court judge, would act and issue a requisition which was handed to the district officer commanding who was to be found in each one of the provinces of the Dominion, directing him to call out from the permanent force first, and if the permanent force were not available to a sufficient extent then from the regular militia, the number of men that would be necessary for the purpose of restoring order in the particular district.
Under the provisions of those various acts during the years of operation since 1876, there have been 59 occasions when troops were called out in aid of civil power. The expenditure thus occasioned to the Dominion government during that period amounted to S556.291.20. The amount recovered by the Dominion government from the muncipalities Which were made chargeable with the cost of bringing out these troops has been only $40,291.65. The House will see that a rather anomalous situation exists. Primarily the duty of maintaining peace and order in this country, under the constitution is vested in the provincial legislatures; they are that part of the organization known at confederation upon whom has been imposed that task. They are to perform that task either by maintaining a police force of their own, as is done in some of the larger provinces, or by imposing upon cities, towns or other municipalities the task of preserving order within their borders through their own police. As a result of the law that has been on the statute book, as I have already pointed out, on 59 occasions we have had to resort to the aid of troops, and on almost every occasion, with the exception of the small amount of $40,000, this has been done at the cost of the whole Dominion. Tha*
Militia Act Amendment

cost should not be imposed upon the whole Dominion. If a difficulty arises in any one of our provinces, then legally and from every other standpoint it is the duty of the government of that particular province to take care of that difficulty. So it is that we propose to amend the law so that hereafter the cost of calling out troops and of their maintenance for the purpose of preventing disorder in any part of the Dominion shall not be, as it has been in the past, a matter of liability on the municipality where the disorder arises, but on the province as a whole. The result will be that the federal treasury will be compensated by each province for the cost to which it has been put in performing this duty on behalf of such province. During that long period, as I say, with those 59 difficulties arising from various causes, there has been grave question as to the possibility of collecting money from the municipalities affected. Different litigations have arisen and protracted lawsuits have gone on. During the war, I think the policy that was adopted was of foregoing the compulsory payment by the municipality of the cost to which the federal government was put. Since the war the policy of both the last government and this has been to claim from the municipality affected the cost to which the federal government has been put. Matters in regard to these questions during the last two years are now in the hands of the Department of Justice. That is primarily the purpose of this measure.
In addition to that, last year a difficulty arose in Nova Scotia, and a commission presided over by Dr. Robertson was appointed which performed its work very satisfactorily to all the people in our province and, I think, generally throughout Canada. They made a recommendation that hereafter provision should be made to amend the law along the line I now propose. They also recommended that in any amendment this House might make, there might be provision that the attorney general of the province should make a report to the Secretary of State of the Dominion as to the conditions which gave rise to the disorder, so that the federal government would be in a position to know officially just what happened.
The course we propose is this. Instead of leaving to the mayor or warden of a particular municipality the responsibility of calling out troops when difficulty arises, we provide that a county court judge, a district judge or a superior court judge, when evidence is submitted to him indicating that the disorder is of such a nature that the aid of military power is required, shall intimate to the attorney general of the province in

which the difficulty arises, the situation; and the attorney general of that province can then, by the issue of a requisition setting out the facts according to a form provided in the bill which I will submit to the House, requisition the district officer commanding the troops in the province in which is the district where the difficulty has arisen. The district officer commanding will in the future as in the past be bound to obey the request of the attorney general. It does seem to me that this is reasonable and proper legislation. The attorney general of the province is the functionary, under our system of government, to whom is deputed the task of administering the criminal law; section 92 of the British North America Act vests in the province the responsibility of administering justice within its own confines. Under this method we shall have a situation in which the country can be assured that due wisdom and care are being displayed in approaching the settlement of any matter involving the intervention of militia; and at the same time the federal treasury will be relieved of an imposition which it never should have borne in the past. With some degree of certainty henceforth the province in which the difficulty arises will be able, indeed will be obliged, to provide the funds necessary to pay for the troops that may be called out.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speechtext:
I am not at all satisfied that this is very wise legislation, at all events from the standpoint of the municipality. In the first place the question of cost referred to by the minister is npt a material point, because this country has, so far, been fortunately free from strikes, riots and from unlawful assemblies as have been spoken of. As one who has been associated with municipal affairs, I think that this legislation is altogether too drastic and too circuitous, inasmuch as it takes away from the chief of police, the mayor, and sheriff in the municipality a function which naturally and logically belongs to them since confederation; and it is in my opinion too dangerous a proceeding for this parliament to interfere in this way with the civil authority. I do not see who is asking for it or what necessity there is for the proposed change. I believe that heretofore considerable tact and good judgment have been displayed by those who have been charged with the maintenance of law and order in our cities and towns. Strikes and other serious disturbances of a like nature have been very rare in Canada and in the

Militia Act Amendment
province I come from. While, on one or two occasions, there have been a few industrial strikes and riots in the city of Toronto, they have been easily settled. It seems to me a most unwise thing to call out the militia unless in the most extreme cases; it is dangerous to meddle with the existing power of municipal authorities in this regard. The chief of police, I am afraid, will be inclined hereafter to fold his arms and to take the view that the judge and the attorney general are the proper officers to keep law and order, and in the event of any disturbance on the streets, as in the case of a street railway strike, he may be apt to show a dangerous indifference. As I say, we have been fortunately free from serious industrial difficulties in this country; the cost to the government of Canada has been practically nil as the municipalities pay it except in one or two cases, such as the strike which occurred in Winnipeg a few years ago and the disturbance which occurred in the province of Nova Scotia as a result of some industrial dispute. I repeat, the cost is not the material thing; and if the government takes away from the proper municipal officer the responsibility which is properly his for the maintenance of law and order in the city, then, when anything happens he may simply refer you to the attorney general who in all probability will be inaccessible. In Ontario, the attorney general as a rule does not live in the city of Toronto; and it is equally difficult to get hold of a judge who may in summer be on a vacation. So that if the police commissioners are either explicitly or implicitly, relieved of responsibility in the matter a dangerous situation is likely to develop at any time. The minister should therefore be exceedingly cautious in seeking to make any change in the present arrangements; the troops ffiould bo called out only as a last resort. Everyone wants to see the law properly enforced; there is no doubt about that. But I am not prepared to grant the necessity for nor wisdom of this change in existing legislation, for I think that on the whole we have had fairly happy relations between capital and labour in this country. The power to put down unlawful disturbances now rests with the mayor, the sheriff and the chief of police who may call the militia to their aid and I do not see why the minister should want to deprive these officers of that power. The people of Toronto pay some $2,500,000 for police protection and it seems to me that the police authorities are well able to take care of them. If the judge should refer you in the future to the attorney general you might find that official absent or he might
await a decision of his government, and possibly when you tried to get in touch with a judge you might find him on holiday. The machinery now proposed is altogether too cumbersome. When a slight disturbance occurred a few years ago in the city of Toronto among the soldiers and there was some disturbance on Yonge street, the civil, authorities requested the militia to keep out of the affair although the regulars were on hand ready if necessary. And what is more, not much damage was done to the property of anybody. Does the Minister of Laboui support this legislation, and has any demand for it come from any labour union o: from the Manufacturers' Association or municipalities? The men who compose the militis are probably very largely taxpayers and many of them may be members of some union oi of the manufacturers. Are these men to be asked to quell industrial disturbances? The local authorities, I repeat, should take care of any' situation that arises in the municipality, and no troops should be brought in unless the circumstances are of such an exceptional and grave nature as to make military interference imperative. The ministers of militia and civil authorities on previous occasions having shown good judgment in connection with matters of this kind, it does seem to me that the law as it is should be left undisturbed. At all events, before this motion is pased the attorneys general of the provinces and the police commissioners should be consulted and the views of the municipalities, and of labour and capital, should be obtained.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
This legislation involves a very drastic change in the law as it has existed in Canada. I have two criticisms to make. One is as to the proposal to constitute the attorney general of the province a sort of court of appeal against the decision of the county court judge to whom application may be made for leave to call out the militia in case of rioting. I do not think it is desirable that the attorney general of any province, who after all is a political officer, should be called upon to review the decision of the judge. The law in respect of the authority of a judge to give orders to call out the troops has worked very well, and I object to the amendment to put the responsibility upon the attorney general of the province.
My second objection is that this legislation will apply practically to only three of the provinces, because of the fact that the only labour disturbances we have had in the Dominion for many years are those arising in the operations of our coal mines in the prov- '
Militia Act Amendment

inces of Nova Scotia, Alberta and British Columbia. It is quite conceivable that labour troubles in any of the colliery sections-and I say nothing as to the merits of the disputes which occasion these disturbances- may have very far-reaching consequences. In Nova Scotia we have large coal areas both in the island of Cape Breton and on the mainland. Our fuel supply is of vital importance not only to the people of Nova Scotia, but to the people of the other provinces where there are no coal deposits, and a strike in any of the mining districts might in its consequences very well reach beyond the locality and affect other parts of the Dominion. Therefore this is not merely a local or a provincial question; it may involve other provinces. Up to the present time, as the minister has said, the municipalities have been liable for the expenses incident to the calling out of the militia. But in this report the law has been more or less of a dead1 letter, for from the figures given to the House by the minister it would appear that a very small proportion of the expenses so incurred has been collected from the municipalities.
Last year the question was discussed on the militia estimates, and it was then suggested that the law should be changed so as to make these costs a charge against the whole country. I do not think it is fair to impose this burden on the province affected, having regard, as I stated, to the far-reaching consequences that may result from labour disturbances in our colliery districts.
There is another section in the proposed resolution to which I have objection, the last, which provides as follows:
That the expenses and costs occasioned by the calling out of the militia shall, pending payment by the province, be advanced in the first instance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by the authority of the Governor in Council, but shall be payable by and recoverable from the province to and by His Majesty as moneys paid by the latter to and for the use of the province at the request of the latter.
It is also provided that these expenses shall be retained out of the annual subsidy to which the province affected may be entitled. Now, the provinces are entitled to certain subsidies in respect of the confederation compact, and these are a part of the provincial revenues. I do not think it is fair that parliament should so amend the militia law as to make the expenses incident to the calling out of the troops payable out of these subsidies. I am quite sure that the sense of the committee would rather be in favour of leaving the subsidies intact, and would prefer to have some other method formulated to secure payment of such expenses by the provincial authorities, if it is ultimately determined [Mr. Kyte.l
that the provinces should become responsible in this respect. On the whole I think that this question might well be left untouched, or if it is considered desirable to relieve the municipalities of the obligation, in my opinion the Dominion should assume the burden, on account of the fact, as I have already pointed out, that disorders requiring the calling out of the militia arise only in the coal-mining areas, which areas are limited to three of the nine provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a
good deal of force in the argument advanced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte). I think possibly the main objection arises out of the first point stated by him; that is to say, you are putting the decision to call out the troops into the hands of a non-judicial officer-the attorney general of the province-and I can see that from very many standpoints this is a very grave objection to the proposed legislation. It is true that the attorney general is charged with the administration of the criminal laws in the various provinces; but the calling out of the militia might be termed an executive act, indeed I think it might be very properly regarded as in the nature of a judicial act, because we all recognize that in the event of a riot the calling out of the militia should only be resorted to after very grave consideration, and therefore the decision to take this extreme measure should only be .exercised with a full sense of the responsibility which it involves.
Now, I observe that in the resolution the calling out of the troops is discretionary on the part of a non-judicial officer. He is, as was stated by the previous speaker, a court of appeal from the requisition of the judicial officer named in the resolution. I do not think that parliament will favourably consider the placing of such power in the hands of a person who in any event is a political official of the provincial government, and I think we would do well to pause before taking this course. In my humble judgment the effect of conferring such power on the attorney general will be entirdy nullified by the succeeding sections of the resolution which place the onus of payment upon the provinces. I venture to say that only in the very gravest instance will the province shoulder the burden of the expense. I have every reason for saying that, because we all know that expenditure of this character, especially in the smaller provinces, is vital to the province. It is true that in the past the law has provided that the municipalities shall recoup the Dominion government for the expenses incurred; but it is also true that the law has

Militia Act Amendment
been more honoured in the breach than the observance. As a matter of curiosity, I think we ought to know what municipalities have reimbursed the Dominion to the extent of the $40,000 mentioned by the minister.
But I do not think that the question of expense is by any means the vital question involved; it is of minor importance; the principle involved is, shall the militia be used in aid of the civil power? That, I think, should only be determined by a judicial officer a non-political officer, a non-partisan officer, a man who is accustomed to weighing facts and evidence, a man who has a sense of responsibility. Not that the attorney general would not have that sense of responsibility, but he is in no sense a judicial officer; and I am opposed to the principle of making it discretionary on the part of any non-judicial officer.
Another point:	Section 1 of the resolution
provides:
That the attorney general of a province upon receiving notification from a judge of a superior or county or district court,-
And so on. Who is to move this judicial officer to requisition the attorney general? Certainly no judge will do it of his own motion. There must be action by the municipal officers if in an organized territory, and in the case of an unorganized territory I am at a loss to know who, under the resolution as it stands, will move the attorney general or the county court judge. So that something is lacking in the first clause of the resolution, and I would ask the minister to give some attention to that.
While it is true that, unfortunately, in the past, most of the disturbances which have been the cause of the calling out of the militia have been in certain coal mining districts, I would like to point out that these districts have been largely urban, well organized, and that there has been a sense of responsibility on the part of the municipal authorities. But I have in mind a coal mining district in a rural locality where there are few if any municipal officers and where the operatives are largely of foreign extraction. What would happen in a community of that character is this:	No local officials
would requisition the county court to make the representation to the attorney general; it would in the last analysis be up to the companies employing these foreign operatives to do so, and we would immediately have the question of capital and labour thrown into the struggle. I am very strongly of the opinion that this matter should be left under judicial control; that it is of too great importance
to be placed in the hands of any political official of any government.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
I go further than the hon. member (Mr. Hanson) and say that the matter should not only be left within judicial control but that the judicial control should be added to by the requirement that the attorney general should join in the requisition along with the judicial authority.
This discussion is interesting to me, because some years ago I moved an amendment that now is the law of this country in reference to calling out the militia. Prior to
4 p.m. that time any two magistrates in any province, no matter where they lived-for instance, in my province they might live at Yarmouth while the trouble might be at Cape Breton-by requisition could call out the militia without conferring with anyone. In the amendment which I moved to a bill introduced by the late Sir Frederick Borden it was provided that in addition to the magistrates there should be action by the mayor of the town or the warden of the municipality, and in case the mayor or warden declined to act, then the requisition could be made by the district court judge.
This resolution favours taking the control entirely away from the municipality, and I doubt very much if that is a proper thing to do. It is scarcely fair to a municipality to provide that the militia may be thrust within their bounds without their having a word to say about it. There may be considerations of importance in that municipality other than those affecting the particular industry in which the strike or labour trouble may occur. I submit that we should make it more difficult to call out the militia, instead of making it easier.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member reads the 'law differently from the way I do, but is it not the law at present that the municipality really has no control?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The present law is that the first requisition to call out the militia must be made by the mayor or warden, but if he refuses then the militia can be called out by the judge of the county or district court. This matter will, of course, be considered more in detail when we have the bill before us. But the general principle does not appeal to me because, as the hon. member (Mr. Hanson) well said, if takes away the judicial control and places it in the hands of an officer who is generally a politician. However brilliant he may be or however able he may be, at the same time he is probably a politician.
Militia Act Amendment

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Is that a term of reproach?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Is not the Minister of
Militia in that position?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Or the
mayor of the town?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: But the judge is not.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: The mayor of the municipality is not.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The militia should not be called out except upon requisition by the mayor or warden of the town or municipality, and in case of their refusing, it should not be called out except upon requisition not only of the judge of the court but of the attorney general as well. We then have the representative of the province and the judicial officer acting together. In other words, it would make it a little more difficult to call out the militia, and I think everybody will admit that the militia should not be called out except in the very last extremity. Every other remedy should first be applied. There may be times, I will admit, when the militia is necessary, but I am inclined to think that on occasions the militia has been called out unnecessarily, or when it might have been better had the militia not been called out.
My objection, therefore,-and I will discuss this matter more fully when the bill is before us-is that we are making it easier to call out the militia; that we are taking away any responsibility on the part of the municipality, and that we are imposing taxation upon people in different parts of the province who are not very much concerned in the matter. For instance, why should the people of the county of Yarmouth or the county of Digby be taxed to pay a per capita share of a provincial tax of $100,000 or $150,000 to take care of unrest, say, in the county of Cape Breton, or in the county of Cumberland? After all, it is the duty of the Dominion government and this parliament to maintain the military law in this country. Had we not better do away with the municipal charge entirely, say it is a farce and let the whole expense be borne by the federal government, which is supposed to maintain law and order so far as the use of the militia goes?
My objection to the last paragraph is just as strong as that made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte). I do not believe we should place any province in the position of a sifspected indigent debtor.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend say that the county of Yarmouth should not pay for the maintenance of law and order in Cape IMr. Logan.]
Breton? From the point of view of the country as a whole does he not think it right that the county of Yarmouth should pay its share in respect to Cape Breton?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS

right to pay for the calling out of the militia in Cape Breton than has the county of Westmorland, New Brunswick, or any other county in the Maritime provinces which is not directly affected. I do think that the last clause is very objectionable-that is to say, paragraph 5 of the resolution which reads as follows:
5. That the expenses and costs occasioned by the calling out of the militia shall, pending payment by the province, be advanced in the first instance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by the authority of the Governor in Council, but shall be payable by and recoverable from the province to and by His Majesty as moneys paid by the latter to and for the use of the province at the request of the latter.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: I am going to ask my hon. friend one more question. I do not want to interrupt him, I have every respect for his argument, but do not law and justice in all provinces have to be enforced by the provincial authorities? But why should Vancouver, for example, be compelled to aid in the enforcement of law and order in the province of Nova Scotia?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: The county of Yarmouth already contributes to the enforcement of law and order in the province of Nova Scotia by bearing a portion of the expense entailed by the maintenance of the provincial police. But I submit that the county of Yarmouth should not be called upon to pay the expense involved by the militia of Canada being called out to maintain law and order in the Dominion any more than any other Canadian county.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
not say that the enforcement of law and justice is a matter of provincial jurisdiction?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Law and justice are matters of provincial jurisdiction, but the militia of Canada are under the control of the Dominion and not under that of any province. Therefore I say that while I should like to hear this matter thoroughly discussed-as it will be in due course-I must state that on general principles I am not in favour of the proposed legislation for the reasons already assigned.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
I should like to ask one
question as to the reasons advanced1 why this

Militia Act Amendment
principle should not be enacted into law. It is desirable that the militia should not be called out except under the most extreme circumstances?	.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Would not the fact that the expense was thrown upon the attorney general-at least the fact of the attorney general remembering that the expense had to be borne by the province-render him still more cautious in accepting requisitions that might be made to him?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
To some extent it might,
but after all it is not always the cost. subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Yes, but it did not seem to me, under your argument, that it would be any more easy to call out the militia than under the present statute. It seems to me that it would be more unlikely that the troops would be called out.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: I cannot agree with you.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence just what the underlying reasons for the proposed legislation are? Is it because of certain occurrences that took place in the county of Cape Breton last summer, and because of certain speeches which the minister made during the Cape Breton North by-election?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: I am afraid that a good many of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken with regard to this matter have been too precipitate in expressing their views. Had they waited until they saw the bill itself I am sure that some of them would not have delivered the addresses they have delivered. I am rather surprised, for instance, to find some of my colleagues from Nova Scotia assuming that this question is one which wholly relates to that province, because during the past ten years I find there have been eleven occasions upon which the troops have been called out in aid of the civil power-twice in British Columbia, three times in Ontario, once in Manitoba, twice in Quebec, once in New Brunswick, and only twice in Nova Scotia. So that the situation is not confined to Nova Scotia by any means.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Would the minister state the expense incurred in each case the troops were called out?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
I have a
statement of the expenditure in each case in a long statement here and shall be very glad to give that information at a later stage However I can give these particulars:
Nanaimo, British Columbia, August 1914, $255,000. Vancouver, Hindoo riots, $1,143.
Windsor, Ontario, 1919, street railway strike, $2,187. Winnipeg, 1919, $196,821.
Quebec, 1922, $184.76.
St. John, N.B., street railway strike, $985.46.
Cape Breton, September 1922, $63,295.
Cape Breton, August, 1923, $99,621.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Would the minister repeat the figures as to the St. John street railway strike?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The amount I have here is $985.46 but I should say that I did not come prepared with the information in detail. If my hon. friends desire fuller or more definite information I shall be very glad to give it at a later stage. I have mentioned these facts to show that the occasions on which the military are called out to aid the civil power arise in all parts of the country and not in any particular section. Furthermore, in the course of ten years of our history there have been eleven occasions on which the act was invoked and they happened in every province of the Dominion except Saskatchewan, Alberta and Prince Edward Island.
My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church), the former mayor of that city, seems to be very much disturbed over the fact that apparently we have taken away some power from the chief of police of Toronto. There is no power vested in the chief of police under the Militia Act as it stands to-day, and I did not altogether catch the point of my hon. friend's criticism. The situation to-day is that under the existing act the mayor of any municipality can of his own volition, if he wishes, issue a requisition to the district officer commanding and call out the troops. It is true that there is a distinction drawn between that act when it is performed by him and the act when it is performed by a judge, because the judicial requisition is especially declared by the act to be such a document as cannot be questioned by the military authorities. It is not desirable, however, that the district officer commanding should be put in the position that he would have to question whether or not the right of a mayor to act was as binding and as conclusive as that of a judge. When disorder occurs and it is possible that lives may be lost and property destroyed, everyone knows that the Canadian people can depend
Militia Act Amendment

upon the proper officials to move in the matter and take such steps as are provided for by law. Of course we all agree that it is most desirable that the military force should not be invoked for the aid of the civil power except in cases of absolute necessity. The use of the military in support of civil power is something that has come to us from the Mother Country. But the situation that arises here is not parallel to similar cases that have occurred in the United Kingdom for the reason that the legislative and administrative machinery over there is concentrated at Westminster. Here the powers are divided under the Confederation Act. The control of militia and defence is vested in the federal authority, whereas the absolute duty is imposed upon the government of a province and it's attorney general of carrying out the police powers within the province. So that we have a situation here quite different from that in the United Kingdom when it comes to calling out the troops to aid the civil power.
Now, it is asserted that the attorney general of a province is a political functionary and that under this proposed enactment he is made a court of appeal from the judges. That is not the idea at all. I am bound to say that I do not know of any attorney general in any province in this country upon whom is not imposed to-day the duty of carrying out the criminal law, of seeing that the prosecutions are properly carried on in every part of the province in which he acts.
I am not for one moment prepared to believe that there is a gentleman occupying the position of attorney general of any one of the provinces who could be said to be so utterly insensible of his duty that he could be termed a politician when considering this serious question. Why is it suggested that he should be?
I am sure that every hon. gentleman who has been vested with responsibility in the past, or who may have it now, or hopes to have it again, so far as federal matters are concerned, will realize that in these matters the situation should be dealt with and the law applied in accordance with the constitution. When a judge intimates to an attorney general or to whatever member of the government may be acting attorney general that it has been called to his attention that a situation exists which in his judgment involves the necessity for calling on the military power, then the attorney general whose duty it is to maintain law and order-not the judge mark you, it never was the function of the judge-must take action. It is the duty of the attorney general who may have at his own command a police force of three or four hundred men, and who will say: "Perhaps the 
judge who calls attention to this situation may not know just the position -we are in. We can summon the police force and deal with the trouble without going to the expense and difficulty of invoking the military power". Is not it fair and reasonable that that duty should be imposed upon him?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: As I understand the matter, the attorney general is made a concurring party in the calling out of the militia-not an appellate party.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Quite so,
my hon. friend has put it more clearly than I could have stated it,-the attorney general is a concurring party, the judge is the official who determines on the facts. The attorney general who has his own police force, mark you -and they exist in all the larger provinces-* can say as to whether or not he can deal with this question with the police force. And is it not only reasonable that that should be the situation? If he comes to the conclusion that the trouble that has arisen is of so grave a nature that it is impossible for him to deal with it with his own police force, then this bill proposes to provide that he shall have the right to invoke the military power. As we are only dealing with bald resolutions which do not deal in detail with the whole question I would suggest to the committee that it would be wiser to leave the questions of detail until we come to the bill. One hon. member spoke about the provisions that exist in regard to calling out of troops in the unorganized parts of the country. With regard to that situation, no change is proposed in the present law. At the present time a district or county court judge or a superior court judge has the power to call out the military in unorganized districts. He will have exactly the same power in the future, with the intervention and co-operation of the attorney general provided for. I refer to the fact that a commission was appointed last summer to inquire into the industrial unrest among the steel workers, which was presided over by Dr. Robertson, who has always been an official of high standing in this country, who dealt with the whole question involved, and made this recommendation.
The commissioners are of opinion that it is desirable that the Militia Act should be amended in such a manner as to provide that a requisition requiring the active militia to be called out for active service in aid of the civil power may be made only by a judge and the attorney general of a province acting jointly in making the same and that the requisition should contain a statement by the attorney general of the province to the effect that he shall as soon as possible, and not later than one week thereafter, cause an inquiry to be made into the circumstances which occasioned the calling out of the active militia and send a report upon the same to the Minister of National Defence.

Militia Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: That report was signed by the three commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Yes Dr.
Robertson, whose high standing is unquestioned, was at the head of that commission, and the other commissioners were men who might be said to be representatives of both capital and labour; and the report which was made was adopted by all three.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Who were the others?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The others
were Mr. J. J. Johnston, former Attorney General of Prince Edward Island and Mr. Fred Bancroft, of Toronto. This is a matter which we should not approach and are not approaching from any standpoint of political feeling. In this matter every party is interested in having the law put upon a proper basis.
In regard to the question whether or not the federal government should assume the full responsibility of all the cost of maintaining military interference where a difficulty arises, I cannot accede to the proposition that has been made that that should be done. Beginning in 1868 the Fathers of Confederation started to lay down the principle in their very first law. Dealing with this question they imposed upon the municipality the cost of maintaining the forces when called out. That has been continued all along. In those early days we did not have the great number of employees' organizations that we have now. Our cities had not been developed. Our smaller towns had not corporate rights. In our province for fifteen years after confederation we had no municipal corporations at all. As the years went by and population increased, and here and there unfortunate difficulties arose in the country, it was found necessary, in the judgment of the men of twenty years ago, to do away with the principle of leaving it to the heads of municipalities to say when the troops should be called out, and they introduced the element into it of the judicial functionary who should have to deal with it. Now, after an interval of twenty years, I think if we only realize what the situation is constitutionally, we will come to the conclusion that in this bill a proposition is made which is reasonable and proper. The provincial government-not the Dominion- is in charge of the task of maintaining law and order and the administration of law. The question as to whether one county in any particular province should be deemed to be treated unfairly if asked to contribute to the cost of calling out the troops is beside the question; because if it is unfair to them
to do so, it is open to the provincial legislature, upon whom the cost would have to fall, to pass legislation themselves for the particular municipality, if they saw fit to do so, assuming the cost of calling out the troops. So, if there is any injustice, the province can relieve it, distributing the cost in any way it sees fit, and I think the provinces are better judges of that than we would be. I think we should endeavour to approach this question with a view to placing upon the statute book, a workable piece of legislation which will deal with this question fairly and reasonably, and if hon. gentlemen desire any further information, I shall be glad to bring it down when we get to another stage.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The situation is not generally understood in that particular. Under the law as it is to-day a judge 'issues a requisition, not to the Department of National Defence, but directly to the officer who happens to be in command of the military district in which the trouble arises. For instance, Judge Finlayson issued a requisi-
Militia Act Amendment

tion to General Thacker, who was in charge of the military district in Nova Scotia, and General Thacker proceeded to act as the law provided, without reference to the department. The law is very clear, it says that he cannot question the requisition when it is made by a judge. Questions of doubt have been involved in regard to matters of this kind, whether the district officer commanding had power to call out troops beyond his own district, for instance whether the district officer commanding in Nova Scotia had power to call troops from other districts beyond. The Department of Justice held that he had, and it has so advised, it has given an opinion to that effect.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Does the Department of Justice advise who has the power of withdrawal? subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS

It is proposed in this bill to remove all doubt on that point by making it clear with whom the responsibility lies, by providing that as the provincial authorities requisition for the troops and have to pay for them, they are the people to intimate when they shall be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
We who are not lawyers do not understand the intricacies of all these statutes and we are liable to get mixed up. We ought to keep in mind the fact that the militia of Canada is not called out primarily to keep or to restore order. It is called out

merely -as an aid to civil power. A municipality Ending itself unable \o maintain order ought to apply to the next higher civil authority, the province. Those constitute the civil powers. The militia should not be called out until those powers are exhausted, and that is all that the statute ever contemplated. Is it unfair to say that both of these civil powers ought to be responsible before the federal power is called in? That is all that this bill proposes.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: Should the municipality not be responsible also?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Certainly. First the
municipality, second t'he province, and if they fail in their duty or if they are unable to cope with the situation, then the militia. That is all that the act ever intended. The difficulty that has existed has been that the municipality in some cases wanted to put the militia ahead, as if it were the duty of the militia to quell any disorder. Then the province unwillingly admitted that it had a duty; if the federal authorities would step in and become the primary power to restore order, that was all right for the province and. the *municipality. But we ought to keep it clearly in mind that it is the duty, first of the municipality, a civil power, to endeavour to restore order. The next higher civil power is the province; if the municipality cannot perform the function, then it should call on the province. And it is only after these two civil powers have exhausted all their forces for the maintenance of peace that the militia should be called on. This bill is to make it more difficult for the militia of Canada to be called out. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) informs me, it is a policing *power. It was never intended that the militia should interfere until every other authority had been exhausted. That being the case, is it unfair, or is it not rather wise, to say that after the municipal authority has exhausted its power, the province is the next higher civil power and it should be brought in to tell the federal authority, the next higher power, that these two powers could not cope with the situation?

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
The people most concerned with this matter are the municipalities of Canada who have been satisfied since confederation with the existing law and are not asking for any change. The question of cost, as I have already said, is not the important thing; what is important is to see that law and order shall be maintained. But how is a judge to know when the services of the militia are required? And is he the proper
Militia Act Amendment
authority to say? Under this legislation the judge is supposed to get in touch with the situation and find out what is going on. He will then have to notify the attorney general and the attorney general, in all probability, wTill take up a lot of time, and may even be absent, he may be out of the country at the time. If this bill becomes law the municipality will not in my opinion be as well off as it is now from the point of view of emergency protection, whereas the municipality will have to pay the bill just the same as the province will assess the local municipality for the entire cost. And all these things fall back upon the municipality in the long run; the municipality has to bear all these burdens. In Ontario in the last few years we had once a Labour-Farmer government which was opposed to anything military; it did not favour the militia, nor did it believe in votes for such purposes. From what source, then, comes the demand for this legislation? Not from the municipalities, or capital or labour. I say there is no demand for it. If there are some small places that cannot afford to pay for the maintenance of law and order then the government should undoubtedly meet such a situation. But under the British North America Act all matters appertaining to the militia and defence are to be decided upon by the people through their representatives in this parliament. And it is dangerous to get away from that principle. If this legislation goes into effect it will in my opinion open the door to a freer use of the militia, and the municipality will pay in taxation without representation and it is likely to suffer not only from the consequences of this interference but also from the expense involved. The municipalities to-day are labouring under a heavy burden of taxation of every kind and they cannot afford to pay any unnecessary bills. I do not think that this legislation is wise; the keeping of law and order is a matter that should rest with the local civil authorities, who at present can take care of it in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
It is satisfactory to note
that something will be done with the control of the militia in respect of its being called
Militia Act Amendment

out in cases of strike. I am not sure whether we can feel satisfied that the bill which the minister has in mind will meet the situation, but I cannot conceive that it will be worse than the present law. There are two points in connection with the act as it is now in force which seem to me to be very unsatisfactory; the first is that the municipal or the local authority has the power to call out the militia against an organization in itself local. That is apt to complicate matters, as indeed it has proved to d'o in many instances. In the case of an industrial dispute it is only natural that there should Ibe considerable heat and that local animosities should creep in. So that those in authority locally, if they happen to disagree with the labour union in the particular city or municipality, will be very anxious to call out some force to settle the matter favourably to themselves. It would therefore be better from that point of view if some other authority a little removed from the immediate disturbance had the final say in the requisitioning of the militia. The next point with regard to the act as now in operation is this:	If the local authorities appear
to foe tardy in exercising their power a judge may call out the militia. I know of no individual who would be more ignorant of the situation than a judge. I do not of course, intend to reflect upon the judges in saying that; but they are entirely removed from the field of action in these cases, not being acquainted with the difliculties that surround industrial life. For that reason, because of their very ignorance of industrial conditions, they are surely the last persons who should be vested with authority in this matter. I am inclined to think that the proposal of the minister, while it may not be adequate, will be an improvement upon what we have at present. As a matter of fact, I do not believe that any act will be adequate which will permit the militia to be called out in cases of industrial disputes; nor do I know of any case in the history of Canada in which, the militia having been called out, there was not more harm done than good, and I doubt whether any occasion will arise in the future when the militia will do more good than they have done in the past. I agree with the statement that has been made by an hon. member that, since we must have an act of this kind, .it will be better to put the control of the situation under the provincial government. But I would go a step further; I would make it more difficult than that, giving also to the federal authority some responsibility, some discretionary power. I would do that in order to make it absolutely certain that before the militia could be called 
out there would be definite assurance that there was real need for it. I would ask the minister whether there is any possibility of his department retaining some responsibility so as to further safeguard the interests of citizens generally before an employer of labour is allowed to call out the militia to quell a disturbance for the creation of which he is largely responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext: The theory of the bill is that the responsibility for maintaining law and order in the country shall be vested in the different provinces and in the law officers thereof. The bill provides that when the provinces find that their local forces are unable to cope with a situation that has arisen they may, following the same practice that obtains in the Mother Country, and by the method prescribed in the bill, requisition the military forces to aid them. The bill sets out in detail t'he methods by which this end is to be attained. It also designates the powers which the district officer commanding, who is the representative of the Defence department, can exercise in the premises. I think my hon. friend had pei-haps better wait until he sees the bill; if then he has any suggestions to make I shall be glad to hear them.

Mr. Chairman, I
am very glad to have the lucid statement by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in regard to the relationship to the different civil powers. I take it that one of the difficulties in connection with the calling out of the militia has been that this action was taken in spite of the advice of the municipalities. There, it seems to me, is one of the real difficulties. When the local authorities, who presumably know something of the situation, have said that they were quite able to maintain law and order, it is possible for a county court judge to ignore their decision and make a request for the militia. That is an intolerable situation, especially when the municipality is later on called upon to pay a bill which it was not responsible for contracting. It has been argued that it is not fair that one municipality should be called to pay for the expense of quelling disturbances in an altogether distinct municipality. If that objection is at all valid, it applies with all the more force to the relationship between the Dominion and the provinces. Why should the whole Dominion be called upon to pay the expense of quelling a disturbance in one particular province? And we are told by the minister that only three provinces have been concerned in these troubles.

subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
Well	then,	why
should the province affected not pay the bill? The province is very largely responsible under our present arrangements for the economic and social conditions that so frequently lead to trouble. We have been told in this House that it is very difficult for us to legislate for an
eight-hour day as that is a provincial matter. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) has referred to the Robertson report. That report not only spoke of the calling out of the militia and made certain recommendations along the lines of this resolution, but it also called attention to the fact that the men were working under very bad conditions, they work eleven and thirteen hour shifts, with every ojther week twenty-four hours of labour on end. Now surely such conditions are intolerable. Further, various industrial disputes investigation committees have told us of the very bad sanitary conditions that prevail in the mining districts. Again and again in connection with the negotiations between companies and men it has been found that the wages paid are altogether inadequate. These are the economic and social conditions which are driving the men to take some action. The only action there seems to be left for them to take is the strike. The province is very largely responsible for the existing situation. Why should not the province pay the bills that arise because of such disgraceful conditions? One of the speakers argued that the attorney general's position was not judicial but political, and implied that a politician could not be trusted in these matters. I would venture to suggest that even under the present act which gives the Minister of National Defence certain authority, the minister's position is non-judicial, and yet he is responsible in the same way as, under the proposed motion, the attorney general would be. But after all, as my colleague (Mr. Irvine) pointed out, the expediency of calling the militia is not a matter which is essentially judicial in character. Such decisions require another type of mind than the purely legal, judicial mind; they require some knowledge of the industrial situation and of the psychology of those who are involved in the dispute.
One hon. member referred to the importance of fuel as it affects the people of the whole Dominion, and suggested that hence this is a Dominion matter. I should like to point out that while fuel may be of importance, and while the dividends of the big companies may also be of importance, the welfare of the men is of still greater importance. That is the point Which, it seems to me, is not fully realized by this House, nor is it recognized in our legislation, nor by the administrative authorities. We can call on the militia to quell a disturbance in order to protect property; we never call on the militia to protect the rights of the men who are working day in and day out for 365 days of the year-when they can obtain the work. That is essen-
Militia Act Amendment

tially the reason why the calling out of the militia does not settle any of these problems; it quells the transient disturbance, but it does not get at the root of the difficulties. It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman,that in referring this matter to the attorney general- perhaps I would rather have had it referred to the lieutenant governor in council-at any rate in referring it to the provincial authorities we are at least helping to saddle the responsibility where it really belongs.
Mr, MEIGHEN: Mr. Chairman, if the law has been as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) has expounded it, I am in favour of an amendment, and I have some sympathy with what the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) said in the first part of his remarks. I have never so understood the law. I certainly do not believe it ever was the intention of parliament that the law should have the effect which the minister states it has to-day. He says that under the law to-day the municipality, by acting through its mayor or reeve, or, failing them, a judge in the municipality having jurisdiction there, may, on the mere say-so of one of these officials that in his belief troops are needed, requisition troops not only in the military district in which that municipality is but throughout the whole of Canada, and that those troops may be kept there just as long as that official likes. Now, that is exactly the statement of the present situation as the minister understands it. Undoubtedly, under the law to-day the municipality, acting through its mayor or reeve, or, failing them-that is, should either of them refuse or neglect or be incapable to act-through any judge, can requisition troops. The statute says, section 81, that the district officer commanding, on receipt of such requisition, or failing him, the senior officer of the active militia, shall call out the active militia or such portion thereof is he considers necessary. The word "shall" s used. The word "shall" is not always imperative, but I am not going to argue at the time that it is not imperative here to the extent of the powers of that senior officer or that district officer as the case may be. But it surely never was the intention of parliament that those powers should be amplified away beyond his own district, that he could reach his hand out, go from Sydney to Vancouver, gather up the active militia both permanent and volunteer, take them across the continent to that particular locality and keep them there as long as he likes. Surely parliament never contemplated such a thing, and I venture to say that governments of Canada have not acted upon that interpretation. The ut-

most that parliament could ever have intended was that upon the requisition the senior officer of the district should send troops as far as he thought they were necessary and so far as they were under his command, that is to say, within his district, and that any troops that went in from outside went in on the responsibility of the government. Let me repeat:	If the Justice department rules-and
to the Justice department of course I must yield in matters of this kind, always reserving this statement: that parliament never so intended; it is preposterous to think parliament so intended-if the Justice department so rules, then the law must go, because the law is absurd. Now the minister proposes that it shall go and that in its place we shall have this situation: The municipality shall send the requisition? No, the municipality hereafter shall have no initiating power. The mayor? No; he is out of the picture too. The reeve? He is equally absent. The judge alone shall send the requisition-a statement of his belief-to the attorney general; the attorney general shall then consider the circumstances and, if he deems action necessary, requisition such action, and that such requisition shall be equally sweeping in its effect, extending beyond the military dio-
5 p.m. trict, beyond the province and throughout the whole confines of Canada. Compliance with such requisition of the attorney general shall be mandatory upon the federal government without the intervention of the last discretion This is what the minister says he proposes to make the law of Canada instead of what exists to-day. Well, I have stated that the law is certainly a preposterous condition of affairs as it exists, if the minister's interpretation is right-it never was so intended. But it is only a little more preposterous than what the minister proposes. In the first place, why is the mayor-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
I am only taking the
minister's answers as he gave them to me, because I was careful to ask him definitely two or three times, his intention. Certainly,

Militia Act Amendment
I repeat, if his intention is persisted in, if he perseveres, he will only have a state of affairs slightly less preposterous than that which exists to-day. I have always thought it was not quite just that on the hypothesis that the municipality was to pay, the initiation of the municipality's responsibility should be in any case shifted from the shoulders of its own officials and vested in a judge. I have never thought that was right. I do not dispute at all that such is the law, or that such has been the law right along. I contend only that that authority is confined within the circumference of the district and never was intended to go beyond. I contend that it is so confined, subject of course, to the higher authority of the Justice department. As to the original intention of parliament, nobody could convince me that it ever was to bring about the situation which has been described.
What is going to be the condition of affairs now? Apparently the municipality's direct responsibility is to go. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is not right in his interpretation of what is intended. According to the Minister of Railways the municipality is to be responsible first, then the province, and if both fail to preserve law and order, then the Dominion. There is no responsibility financially under this new legislation to devolve upon the municipality; the province is to be wholly responsible. Of course the province could so legislate as to distribute that responsibility, or localize it, but the minister's act comes into effect at once and no province has such legislation. I suggest that the minister should consider postponing the coming into operation of the act until the provinces have an opportunity to place the ultimate responsibility where heretofore it'always has been.
Next, assuming that the provinces will want to bring back the old condition of affairs-the ultimate responsibility on the municipality-I do not see why the mayor and the mayor's officers should be wiped away and the judge alone put in their place. These two objections I advance now, but here is the one that is to me far more formidable and unanswerable: By what right is any province going to summon the Dominion parliament, the Dominion government, to gather its militia from all over the Dominion, land them in that province and keep them there as long as the officers of that province like? We will assume, for example, that Nova Scotia is the first to act. Alberta may 182
be, Saskatchewan may be-the farmers there sometimes assume a militant attitude; but suppose Nova Scotia acts first: Nova Scotia becomes so alarmed that they believe the whole permanent militia of Canada-"active militia" is the way the act reads and the way it is going to read-should go in there. Last summer, for no very great cause, they thought they should go right from Winnipeg-if I am wrong I would like to be corrected-right out from Manitoba. Well, it would not take very much to have (hem come right from Vancouver; the Nova Scotia authorities can bring the troops and keep them there. Now suppose they do. The minister says "Oh, they are going to pay for it." Very well, but there may be trouble in Alberta the next week and how are we going to take care of that? There may be trouble in British Columbia. The Winnipeg situation may be repeated. What does the minister propose in that event? He is going to divest himself of every possible discretion, he is going to put himself utterly powerless in the hands of an attorney general, and if he does he will find himself helpless and disarmed should a certain situation arise comparable with the first. Now, I never have believed that, there was no discretion in the Dominion government. I have always believed there was in so far as the troops are concerned beyond the district affected; and f insist that in this legislation discretion to this extent at least be preserved, that the federal government be not under command of any provincial authority to send troops into that district beyond those within the military district affected. Secondly, that beyond that circumference the power, utterly unfettered, remain in the hands of the responsible federal authorities.

The government will accept any reasonable suggestion that may be advanced in order to make this bill thoroughly workable. Because this is really not a matter upon which there should be any political division; we are all approaching the subject with a view to framing the best possible law that can be enacted.
My right hon. friend has made a very good point as to whether it might not be desirable, should this legislation become law, of postponing its coming into operation. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TROOPS IN AID OF CIVIL POWERS
speechtext:
There is just this I
would add in reply to what the minister has said. He admits! that the district officer commanding is to have this full sweeping authority under the amendments as proposed but he says that subsequently reasonable amendments to the bill may be accepted. He states it is not very likely that the district officer commanding would summon the militia from the ends of the country because the volunteer militia are available. Does he re-
member that the reason the permanent force are sent first is that they are the most efficient force; secondly, because that does not entail any cost upon the municipality as will be the result in this case. If the law is passed as proposed the district officer commanding will call out the permanent force and what will be the result? If the situation is just a little worse than it was in Nova Scotia he will summon the troops from Vancouver. What a fine situation would then arise if a difficulty occurred in Alberta or in British Columbia. The men who would be there would be these active militia, who would be paid day by day, without the support, without the experience, without the training and certainly without the efficiency of the permanent force. It would leave the rest of the country utterly stripped, and the government would stand stark and helpless, unable to do anything.
