speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A reorganization is proceeding in the surveys of the department. We have discussed this a great many times, and in the amalgamation of the work I have been seeking to bring about in the department we have been endeavouring to cut down the staff. A number of the older officials are seeking superannuation, and the staff will be cut very materially. As a matter of fact, I cannot say offhand, but I know that we have three or four positions in that division which it is not our intention to fill. Of course the younger men in the service are taking the higher positions, but the Assistant Director General of Surveys, while not a temporary appointment, is more or less of that nature. Our director has been ill for the past three or four months, and is quite an aged gentleman. We are not adding to that particular branch of the work but rather decreasing it.
Is the present position filled, and if so how long has it been filled?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Thomas Shanks occupies that position.

How long has he
occupied that position?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since April first.
Is his appointment subject to the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Did he sit for examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How long since the examination took place?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the exact date at which the competition took place but it was some time last fall. I cannot remember the exact date. A number of the officers of the department wrote in that examination. The Civil Service Commission appointed him.

'Was the position
occupied prior to Mr. Shanks' appointment and by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it was temporarily occupied by Mr. Peters.

For how long?
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps it is a mistake to say it was occupied. Mr. Peters had been carrying on this work ever since he had been brought from Calgary. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) raised the question of the allowance that was paid him for assisting with the reorganization. He was never appointed to the position. He was drawing the salary he had been drawing when located at Calgary.

I understand that the examination for the position of Assistant Director General of Surveys was made some time last fall, but notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Shanks was the proper person to appoint, he was kept out of the position because of the desire of someone to keep Mr. Peters in that particular position. Has the minister any explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know anything about that. The Civil Service Act is specific in that regard. In the case of post office appointments, I have one case in mind at the moment in which the appointment was made by the Civil Service Commission where it was not approved by the Postmaster General. Approval has to be given by the Governor in Council, but the recommendation comes from the department. In looking up the act I find that there is nothing that the department can do except to refuse approval. They might do that, but then that creates a situation that is impossible. There must be a trial of the individual passed upon by the Civil Service Commission. If he is unsatisfactory, then, of course, the department have authority, for which they must give reasons, for refusal to make the position permanent. But under the act they must accept the decision of the Civil Service Commission and appoint for six months the party named by them.
Did the department withhold approval of the appointment of Mr. Shanks?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was not
aware of that. That may be true.

As reported on page 2510 of
Hansard, I asked certain questions dealing with the appointment to a vacancy in the Fort Smith district agency. The material portion of the questions asked are as follows:
1.	Is Mr. C. S. MacDonald, Dominion Land Surveyor, an employee in the Department of the Interior?
2.	Was Mr. MacDonald appointed to the position of District Agent of the Northwest territories, at Fort Smith, N.W.T.?
3.	If so, is Mr. MacDonald fulfilling the duties of that office? If not, why not?

The answer to the first question was: Yes. The answer to the second question was:
He was notified by the Civil Service Commission to report on receipt of instructions from the department.
The answer to the third question was:
No. Has not got necessary administrative experience.
I want to draw that to the attention of the minister because, as he would know, the Civil Service Commission is the final body under the statute which determines as to the qualifications of the individual, and no department has any right to say that, because this man, after having been chosen by the Civil Service Commission, has not the necessary administrative experience, he shall, therefore, not occupy that particular position. That is a direct contravention of the statute, and I simply draw the attention of the minister to it, because I am sure, under the circumstances and realizing the matter, he will see that justice is done in the premises.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think there must be some mistake with reference to the answer, because it is very clear that the department has not authority to appoint someone else in place of an appointee of the Civil Service Commission.

The answer is to be found on page 2510 of Hansard. The further question which I did not read, because it was not material to the point I wished to make, is as follows:
(a) What person, if any, is acting as District Agent at Fort Smith, N.W.T.? (b) What salary does he receive and (c) from what fund is he being paid ?
The answer is:
(a) J. A. McDougal;	(b) Salary', $2,700, living
allowance, $1,500; (c) Northwest Territories Administration vote.
The point I want to make is not that somebody else was put in the position, but that the Civil Service Commission gives a certificate to another individual to fill that position, and the department comes along and says: No, we will not place him in the position because he has not the necessary administrative experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know anything about the particular circumstances, but I imagine that in that case McDougal could not draw his salary. I will make full inquiry. I think there must be something wrong with the inference that the Civil Service Commission appointed! MacDonald.

The answer is perfectly clear.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are checked very closely by the audit, and if that were the case, McDougal would not be able to draw his salary. I shall, however, make full inquiry. I do not want to get into a controversy about the matter at the moment.

Are all the increases
shown statutory increases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

There appear to be
some decreases in salary. I notice on page 76 an item: Publicity agent, this year, $1,920; last year $2,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That can
come about only in one way. There must have been a change, but the gentleman is at the minimum of the class instead of getting towards the maximum. The salary is fixed for that particular position with a maximum and a minimum. Of course, when a man moves out to some other position and a new man takes his position, he begins at the minimum salary.

On page 77 there is
another item: Assistant Dominion land surveyor, this year, $2,555; last year; $2,562.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There have
been a number of changes in the surveying staff; there have been a number of resignations, and undoubtedly the same answer applies in this case. This may not be the minimum salary, but it will be a lower salary than that which the former occupant of the position was receiving.
The same thing applies to all the other cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that it might be a difference in the date of the statutory increase. They do not all date at the beginning of the fiscal year. That might account for the smaller amount, but usually that happens because the occupant is beginning at the minimum of the class.

I suppose the same
thing would apply to other cases where there have been decreases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that there might be a difference in the date at which the statutory increase takes place. For instance it might not take place on the 1st April; it might occur on the 1st July or the 1st October.

There has been no
attempt to decrease any of the salaries in this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We could
not decrease salaries. The salaries for the positions are fixed.

Are homestead inspectors
included in this appropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

How many are maintained
in the three prairie provinces and what salaries are they receiving?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We passed
that item, but I will try to get the information for my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister says that
he could not decrease the salaries. Will he tell us who could?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend will agree with me that the Civil Service Commission fix the minimum and maximum salaries for any particular position. The minister has nothing to do with salaries, except those of his secretary and the deputy minister. They are the only positions over which he has control, with the exception of positions the remuneration for which is under $200. I think that is the amount fixed now. The salaries of all other positions are fixed by the Civil Service Commission, with a maximum and minimum for the class.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
At the request of The
government. If the government wants the Civil Service Commission to revise the salaries down, all it has to do is to request them to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No country has put out
of the hands of the government or of parliament the power to determine the salaries it pays to its employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
quite right. The minister or the deputy minister can make recommendations. In fact, he has made recommendations and the recommendation goes to the Civil Service Commission, but the commission adjudicate on that recommendation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They do not adjudicate
except to this extent:	They make recommendations to the government which the government may accept or not as it sees fit. But the general scale of salaries is a matter which is in the hands of the government, and the
Supply-Interior

Civil Service Commission, merely makes a classification of the individual salaries. If at any time the government wants to reduce the total, all it has to do is to intimate to the commission that a reduction of 10 or IS per cent, as the case may be, is required, and the Commission will classify accordingly. When a general scale comes before the government the government passes it or sends it back.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
agree that the government goes as far as that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am having a little experience with the commission now in regard to the postal employees. The government or the minister or the deputy minister can make a recommendation, but the commission fixes-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission does not fix anything; it only makes recommendations to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, let us say it recommends. But what does the act say about the powers of the government? The government may approve; but if it does not approve, what then?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It refers the matter
back.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But if there is to be a continuous reference back and forth there is going to be an impasse. The Civil Service Commission makes a recommendation to the minister or the deputy minister naming, or fixing, or suggesting such and such salaries and1 remunerations as it sees fit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Only the government
can finally determine what the general scale shall be. If the government does not approve of a scale because it is too high it can refer the matter back to the Civil Service Commission. The minister knows as well as he is sitting in his seat that if the government felt that a general scale was five, or ten or fifteen per cent higher than it should be under present conditions, all that would be necessary would be to so represent to the commission and ask them to submit a scale reduced individually in accordance with that general reduction. The minister knows that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Would that not be considered undue influence?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not at all; it is entirely in the hands of the government to say what the general scale ought to be.
fMr. Meighen.]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend suggest that the commission is bound to accept that recommendation from the government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad
to know that, because I cannot construe the act in that way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister knows
that the Civil Service Commission is a classifying body; but the general scale is something which is in the hands of the government, subject to parliament. The minister, to get out of some trouble that threatened in the post office department, referred the scale back to the commission for revision. The commission revised it but the government did not say whether they Wanted it up or down. Is it not a fact that the commission asked whether the government wanted the scale u,p or down?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not that
I am aware of.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister will make inquiries he will find that to be the ease. But I could not see how in the world the commission could be expected to make a revision, having just done so, unless there was an intimation as to what the government wanted. I made formal inquiries to find out the facts and I discovered that the government did not inform the commission what it desired to have done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend was in the government which passed the act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes; and the act is all right. But we never said that we were helpless under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
right hon. friend suggest that the government has any control over the question as to what the salaries shall be?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In so far as the general
level of salaries is concerned. If the government think that the general scale in any case is too high, all they have to do is to inform the commission accordingly. And I challenge them to try that out. If the government are of the opinion that salaries are too high, I ask them to submit a requisition to the commission, as they did in the case of the Post Office Department, only intimating, in this instance, the reason for the revision. Let them say: "We want the salaries revised because we be-

Supply-Interior
lieve they are too high; we think there should be a reduction of 10 or 15 per cent and we ask you to make a recommendation with that in view." Let the government try that and see if the commission will not respond.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I usually
agree with my hon. friend but I cannot on this occasion. .

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Try it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What in
the name of heaven was the commission appointed for if it is to be a rubber stamp in a matter of this kind? I am not a lawyer and in construing the act I am apt to make terrible mistakes. But I take the intent of the act to be that the commission should exist for the very purpose of taking this matter from the hands of the government. I quite understand that the government is ultimately responsible.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But on the other hand what is the sense of having a commission if the government are to have absolute control to this extent?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister knows that
the commission has two functions, one, to classify and the other, to appoint, subject in every case to the approval of the government. But it has no final authority in any case. These two functions of the commission are considerable; but surely no one will suggest that parliament has put into the hands of that body the uncontrollable power to write cheques at whatever dimensions it sees fit against the treasury of Canada in favour of the service of Canada. It cannot possibly do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend suggest that if the minister or the deputy should recommend that a salary of, say, 84,500 be paid a certain individual, it is the duty of the commission to fix that salary?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I never said that, and
that is not the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What my
hon. friend is saying seems to be to that effect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What I am saying is
that the responsibility for the general level of salaries rests with the government, and if they feel that it is too high they can refer the matter to the commission with a request that it be reduced by a certain percentage. If they make that recommendation the commission will undoubtedly act upon it. The commission will then by rts classification .adjust the individual salaries to meet the
total reduction. The reason I went into this matter was that the minister of a department, to get out of a trouble that was his own, made a reference to the commission.
I asked the minister concerned and the Prime Minister whether they had indicated to the commission just What they really wanted- whether an upward or a downward revision

and they said, no; they virtually said, "We just threw the thing at them." I therefore wondered what in the world the commission would do, and upon making inquiries in the regular way I learned that they had never been informed by the government as to whether the revision was to be up or down, or by how much. So that I am speaking of my own knowledge when I say that if the government really think the general scale is too high, all they have to do is to say so and they will get a classification apportioning the individual salaries so as to meet the lower level.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can well
understand that the commission would pay a great deal of attention to any recommendation from the government regarding a general revision of an entire scale of salaries. One can easily understand that. But that is not the point I have been trying to make. I understand that the commission can go even a great deal further, in a general way, than my right hon. friend argues this afternoon. But the government need not accept any recommendation of the commission, and it would be absurd to suggest anything else.

Is it not a fact that
in connection with the revision of salaries of postal employees the commission reported three several times to the government and three several times the government returned to the commission the recommendation it had made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend is correct in making the statement twice, not three times.

Then for what reason
was the report returned to the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not under this vote: this is the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer that question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: To gain time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

I simply mention this,
Mr. Chairman, because the minister has referred to it himself.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not in this vote anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was referred to by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It was used by the
right hon. leader of the opposition as a measure of comparison.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	My memory may be
wrong then, but I think Hansard will bear me out. As I understand, the minister said he bad some trouble with the postal employees. However, if you rule out any discussion, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No, I do not. By way of comparison, it might be used, but I say you cannot address to the minister under the Interior vote an inquiry relating to the postal service.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	Then I will ask this
question:	Is the revision of the salaries of
the Interior department and of the Department of Indian Affairs being proceeded with, and what stage has it reached?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
tell my hon. friend whether the revision has commenced or not, but all salaries which were affected by the bonus are under revision.
Mr. MeQUARRIE: Has the Civil Service Commission made any report as to any other salaries than those of the postal employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not that I am aware of.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	Would the minister
be aware if they had made a report?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think so.
There has been none so far as I know.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	Then what is the
reason why the postal employees' salaries have been taken up first?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The order
in council, which was laid upon the Table, asked that the postal employees and the customs employees be dealt with first.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	Of course that hardly
answers the question. Why was it the government desired the commission to take up the postal employees' salaries first? Was it on account of the threatened strike?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Naturally
that was part of the reason.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	That was the reason.
When I asked the Prime Minister the other day he answered that that had nothing to do with it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When a readjustment was asked for by the postal employees a serious situation arose-for I think my hon. friend will agree with me that a strike of the postal employees would be a serious situation-and I think he will also agree that it was well that their salaries should be dealt wtih as soon as possible.
Mr. MeQUARRIE:	That is the way it
appealed to me, and I was rather surprised at the Prime Minister's answer. I must say that the answer which the minister has just given appears to me much more reasonable. In regard to the revision of the salaries of other employees of the Civil Service, there is. as I understand it, great complaint that the revision is not being proceeded with and that the men are not receiving any consideration whatever. Has the minister heard of any such complaints?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have had
no notice of any complaints in the three departments of which I have charge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the minister say
what his attitude is towards a strike in the Civil Service; does he think it should be treated the same as a strike by private employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I do
not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What would be the government's attitude?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
think this is the place to commit ourselves in face of the difficulties which confront us; but it seems to me, that policemen and civil servants are in a different category altogether from people engaged in industrial disputes; they are servants of the Crown. It is rather a serious thing for these men to resort to a strike. On the other hand, one cannot say that they should foe denied the right to protect themselves. However, that is my general attitude.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Nobody disputes that.
Mr. MeQUARRIE: WTe will suppose that the employees of the Interior department were threatening to strike:	Would the minister and the government then take up the revision of their salaries next after the consideration of the salaries of the postal employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is very thirsty for information. Speak-

Supply-Interior
ing from memory, I think the order in council requested that if possible the salaries of the postal employees and the customs employees should be dealt with first.

But the salaries of the customs employees are not being dealt with,
I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer that question, I do not know.

There is no report
from the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say that the same request for expedition has been asked all along the line. I can* hardly believe that the Civil Service Commission is simply doing nothing.
What is the government doing to assist expedition?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as I know, the government have no knowledge that there is a complaint.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has not the government refused already to accept two reports from the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is asking another question entirely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, that is the same
question. First the minister said that the government instructed the Civil Service Commission to use all expedition so as to get all possible light on the subject, but he said a little while ago that the commission reported once and the government referred the report back, and after the commission reported again the government again referred the report back. So the government's instructions are a great deal better than its actions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Refusal is
hardly the word.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The government referred the report back. So far as expedition is concerned, it amounts to the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not
objecting, but I do not think refusal is the proper word to use at this juncture with respect to the revision of the salaries of the postal employees.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is equally effective.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Our idea is
to try to arrange an amicable settlement, and I think my right hon. friend will agree that that is the proper course to pursue. I happen to be rather vitally interested inasmuch as I am Acting Postmaster General, and
therefore that is the only object I have in view. On the other hand, I do not want the idea to go out that because these men met and took a strike vote that was the sole reason why they were dealt with at once. Undoubtedly it was one of the reasons so as to see if an amicable adjustment could not be made. But I would very much resent compulsion from the post office or any other employees. At the same time I want to make it very clear that I am desirous to give them just, fair and equitable treatment.
What were the other reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend seems to be desperately anxious to obtain information on this point. I think my hon. friend will readily agree that the Acting Postmaster General has a rather difficult situation on his hands, and he will appreciate that words which I may utter here may be used outside the House, and perhaps imperil an equitable adjustment of the trouble. I hope it will be settled within a day or two, and settled amicably. I cannot prevent these employees from going on strike, and I am not making any threats about it. I am trying to make this adjustment, but my hon. friend is pressing for information that I have had to refuse to give to the representatives of the employees.
I understand the minister to say that the threatened strike was only one of the reasons for giving preference to the postal employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The other
reason is this; the postal employees have been pressing for an adjustment for the last two years, and so have the customs officers.
Other departments as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be so, but frankly I was not aware that other departments had been doing so. Undoubtedly, individuals and groups in other departments have been but there has not been the request for a general adjustment such as the postal employees and the customs officials have asked for.

The Amalgamated
Civil Servants of Canada have had their representatives here; have they not requested that the revision of their salaries be proceeded with immediately? Are they not pressing for the other departments just as much as the Postal Employees' Association have been pressing for theirs?
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If that is the fact I was not aware of it-not to the same extent.

The minister stated
that some seventeen positions in his department had been abolished on his recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And not on the recommendation of the Civil Service 'Commission-that is as I understood him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is correct.

If the hon.

He is reading a statement with reference to civil government and that is the vote we are discussing at the moment. I am doing my level best to ascertain where economies can be instituted and I hope to be able to make reductions. We have reduced the staff by seventeen employees under the head of civil government and I think I can reduce it more because it is needless for me to say to my hon. friend that there is not as much business done now as there was in the year when the department had a thousand employees. We have reduced the staff by seventeen and we have a number of retirements of elderly people in view. I do not wish to say that I am forcing these people out, they are retiring' voluntarily and their positions will not be filled. I propose to reduce the staff just as fast as I can, because this is a very large department and it costs a lot of money. My hon. friend must bear in mind that the unfairness of the article from which he is quoting consists in this, that no allowance is made in it for the difference between the salaries prevalent to-day and those in the days as regards which comparisons are made. It is quite fair to make the comparison as to numbers as long as you compare the volume of work in carrying on the department. I have not increased the civil government staff of the Department of the Interior by a single individual. Reductions have gone on every year since I have taken office.

The only reduction

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

as being so remarkable in view of those charges and similar ones that have been made of extravagance on the part of the government, is that the minister should not have ascertained how much his department is actually costing in salaries.

friend is welcome to do so, but there is nothing in MacLean's Magazine that deals with the general departmental vote. It deals with the civil government vote, of the department. The Civil Service as regards numbers has been reduced by 300 employees. There were 1,000 people according to the statement made by Mr. O'Leary.

I have not a reduction; I have an increase all the time. The balance of the statement is as follows:

This is the indictment of the department:
No one will seriously argue that the administrative requirements of the Interior are any greater to-day than they were in 1913; yet the fact remains-as these figures show-that the department has increased its staff between that time and the present by more than 500 officials, and has advanced its cost to the public by about $1,250,000 a year. And this, be it remembered, does not include officials and salaries of the Interior department in the outside service, and has nothing whatever to do with the Department of Immigration. Taken all in all it is one of the worst examples of overmanning in the government service.
Those statements are either true or untrue. If they are true, then the department is seriously overstaffed. What is the minister

doing to meet that situation? He is asking this year for practically the same amount of money as was required last year. There is no reduction at all except this $4,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is not the case, for this reason. As I pointed out to my hon. friend before, if he will carefully examine the statement, he will find that there is a reduction of over $700,000 in the general vote for the department and a very large part of the staff is paid from that vote. We have $1,500,000 voted for 816 employees who are under civil government and whose names appear in this lidt. We have a reduction there of $4,000. We have been reducing the staff very rapidly and the statement contained in MacLean's Magazine that we are overmanned because of an increase of staff is quite beyond a reasonable statement of the true condition of affairs. My hon. friend, perhaps, will say that, because of a reduction of the work of this particular department, we should have a tremendous reduction in staff. To some extent that is true and as fast as we can reduce, we are doing so. But some people forget that this department is cleaning up such accounts as we were discussing the other day: advances for seed grain, loans to settlers and homesteads still to be inspected, although not at the same ratio because we have not homesteading going on. That particular activity in the department is the place where we can reduce most rapidly, but there is no reduction in our work in the other direction. I do not say that I cannot make considerable reductions in the staff; I propose doing so and I am doing so all the time, and also making a reduction in expenditure. I claim that a reduction of three-quarters of a million dollars in one year is meeting at a pretty reasonable rate the clamour for reduced expenditure. I cannot but think that I have done all that is humanly possible in the way of reduction this year. I am not going to say that it is ended, because I think I can make more reductions, and I propose to make more-more reduction in this particular staff as well as in the outside service-as fast as the work decreases. The statement that the department has been hugely overmanned, I do not think I or my predecessor would admit. It has been reduced in my time, but there is a tremendous amount of work performed in the Department of the Interior. If my hon. friend has time some day just to look into the activities of the department, he will discover how much territory we cover. We are administering land and resources in three provinces in the prairie belt, in his own province, in the Peace river block.

That cannot be done without a staff at the head office or without a staff in the provinces.
I confess that the reduction in the provinces this year, the closing up of the land office at Saskatoon, the cutting out of sub-offices, and the closing of the one at Battleford, with the consequent reduction of $700,000 in the estimates, have been the subject of severe criticism on the ground that we are not giving the service to the people. Let me say however that I am doing the best I can with a very large department.

Does the minister
say that there has been a reduction of $750,000 in the cost of civil government in connection with his staff?

No; this
official is transferred from another position.

The minister also intimated that, according to the statement in the estimates, there had been a saving of $20,500 by reason of a number of officials having been superannuated. But the fact is that these officials are really transferred to another department of the government, as one might say; they are put on the superannuation list and, as the minister admits, the cost in connection with them is about seven-tenths of what it was previously. So that after all there is not a saving of $20,500 in that connection as we have been given to understand; there may seem to be a saving to the minister's department of that amount but it is not a saving to the country. Some time during the session I placed on the order paper the following question:
What is the total amount in annual salary of the new appointments to the Civil Service since December 29, 1922?
The answer was that, in connection with the Department of Interior, there had been an increase during that period of $227,761 under the head of civil government. In 1922 the increase was $114,904, in 1923 $105,149-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman is not attributing this to an increase in staff.

The question speaks for itself. Let me read it again:
What is the total amount in annual salary of the new appointments to the Civil Service since December 29, 1922?
That was the question, and as I have stated, the increase for 1922 was stated to be $114,904, for 1923 $105,149 and for 1924 $7,708. Now, this does not indicate any decrease in the cost of the department in connection with staff, if these figures are correct. And this is the only way we have of arriving at any clear and definite understanding as to what is going on in the department. It is well understood that there is an enormous increase in the Civil Service of the country, and the great need in Canada to-day, not only in the administration of public affairs but in every other sphere, is economy; particularly in connection with the government of the country, the paramount need is economy in the Civil Service. We must reduce our expenditures in every possible way if we are to make ends meet. Yet we are daily receiving notices from the Civil Service Commission of appointments to be made in the various departments of government. I would suggest to the government that instead of making new appointments, they utilize some of the superfluous assistance which is at present employed in some of the departments; rather than create new offices the government should transfer from those departments that are over-manned, to others in which more help is required, such officials as *at the present time are unnecessary. But this is not being done; on the contrary, advertisements are appearing frequently from time to time in regard to fresh appointments that are being made. Why do the government not transfer these superfluous officials from one department to another and economize in that way? There must be something radically wrong in the system when these new appointments are being made with such frequency. I can quite understand the hardship it would be to throw out of employment civil servants who have spent the greater part of their lives in the service of the country and who would find it exceedingly difficult to compete with people in private life. I would not advocate any such thing; nor do I think such a policy is necessary. But it is imperative that the government should practise economy in this matter; there should be some common sense in the filling of positions. When therefore some official is required for

a new position that is to be filled, why not transfer somebody who is not needed in some other department? Men are being superannuated to-day who are just as useful to the country as they were some years ago, and possibly more so in view of the experience they have acquired. Many of the new appointees are men of over sixty. I am not referring to the Civil Service in Ottawa; but I have in mind just now a man of upwards of sixty-five whose hearing and sight were both bad who was appointed to a position only a short time ago through the Civil Service Commission acting under instructions from the government, while at the same time other men who are more competent are being superannuated. There is no sense in this; why not take the matter in hand and, where there are idle officials in one department, transfer them to some branch which is in need of extra help, rather than go to the expense of a new appointment. If this return is correct I am inclined to think that the minister is not frank with the committee to-night; at any rate there is something wrong somewhere. I have put questions to other ministers in this regard when their estimates have been before the committee and I have received answers similar to those which we have been given tonight, that the number of officials is being reduced. But the returns tabled in answer to questions do not bear this out. We must reduce overhead expenses in this country if we are to carry on; that is obvious to every one. I am not in favour of turning out those who have served the country for a number of years to the best of their ability. At the same time, however, those who are found to be superfluous could very easily be utilized by being transferred to some other department. This would be much better for all concerned. Certainly those civil servants who have been in the service of the country for such a length of time are entitled to every consideration at the hands of the government and of the people, especially when we reflect on their inability to meet competition in a department of life which would be entirely new to them. Why, the very hours which they are called upon to serve constitute a handicap to them; they are not accustomed to a day's work, and they would be at a disadvantage if they were turned out of the service.
Mr. HEALY; Put them in the Senate.

I think the minister ought to give us some explanation as to the necessity for this new appointment of an Assistant Director of General Surveys at a salary of $4,350. There are areas of land 
unsurveyed in the Northwest Territories which, it seems to me, it is not absolutely necessary should be brought under cultivation just now. If there is anything of which we have a surplus in Canada to-day, it is farmers. I noticed an article in a New York paper a short time ago referring to the exodus of farmers from the United States to Canada, and particularly to northwestern Canada. They pointed out that there were people who had been engaged in grain growing in the United States and would not adapt themselves to diversified farming there, and that they had gone to Canada in order to obtain cheap land.

Is the hon. member
opposed to any more farmers coming to this country?

I do not think my
hon. friend's question is pertinent to the subject we are discussing. I am referring to an article which appeared in a New York paper pointing out that the exodus of American farmers to Canada was decreasing, giving the numbers for several years past, and stating that the great problem in the United States was the necessity for reducing the acreage under wheat, as they were growing too much wheat, and that the country was glad to get rid of these grain growers who would not adapt themselves to general farming and were therefore going to western Canada. The article stated that the United States had secured for their industries one-third of the Canadians who had so distinguished themselves overseas, and it compared the advantages which had accrued to the country in the exchange. Now, I do not understand why it should be necessary to create this new position of Assistant Director General of Surveys. I think it would be much more to the advantage of the Dominion to see that our farms are properly cultivated rather than to bring new areas under cultivation. For that reason I would ask the minister to inform the committee why it is necessary that this new position should be created. Also, whether the statement furnished in response to the question which I submitted is correct or not.

I was under the impression that my hon. friend was misled by the idea that the return covered new positions -which had been created since 1922. That is not the fact, because really we have been reducing the. staff. I am not claiming any particular credit for it, as the war created a great deal of extra work, and necessitated additions to the staff, but the general reductions in the staff, I think, run between four thousand and five thousand according to the last returns. The numbers I have read represent transfers. Now wherever we have a person who can take a position in some other branch we are trying to place him there, always with the consent of the Civil Service Commission, because we have in our department a representative of the commission who is going through the staff all the time and assisting us in this work.

Would the return which
the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland! has referred to include transfers such as the minister is now speaking of?

I do not
think it would.

It would mean either
new positions created or vacancies filled from outside altogether?

One or the other.

speechtext:
They are
new people who come into the service to take new positions.

I think tone criticism
which may be made of this department, as well as of others, is that while it is true the minister has in his general estimates shown a saving of three-quarters of a million dollars, he has not shown a corresponding saving in the overhead, and this is the one thing which the country is criticising very severely. It cannot be said with -any degree of accuracy that a reduction of seventeen in the number of officials in this department is in any way commensurate with the reduction in the service of the department as a whole, neither can it be said that a saving of $4,000 in overhead salary is commensurate with the decreasing work the minister has himself acknowledged. I have no doubt he has made a good start with respect to the outside service, but I do not think he will claim-and he has not claimed really here to-night-that he has made very much progress with respect to the inside service in Ottawa. That may not be the minister's fault, but a reduction of the inside staff ought to be his -aim, and it is what the country is asking for. It is felt that there are altogether too many civil service officials in the head offices of these various departments. I think the minister if he is candid will agree with my criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The centre
of the whole organization is here at Ottawa, which may or may not be good business, but nevertheless it is here. The outside service is curtailed wherever possible. For example, all the branches, and there are a great number of them) are run from Ottawa. Of course, as my hon. friend will understand, -that necessitates a fairly large head office staff, but every individual of that staff is on this list, and naturally this will be the last list to be cut. Undoubtedly I hope to make reductions, because I frankly admit that I think the work in this department will decrease year by year; therefore there should be a corresponding reduction in the staff. But I do claim that a cut of three-quarters of a
Supply-Interior

million dollars in the Department of the Interior is a pretty fair showing. With that before the committee I fail to see why I should be criticised so severely because someone on the outside undertakes to write a magazine article without putting himself to the trouble of going through the department. The Audit Board under the powers granted them will attend to reductions, and I trust they will do the work thoroughly. At the moment in this huge' staff of eight hundred odd people I do not know that I am over-manned to the extent of even one person. Of course, some members of the staff are asking for superannuation, and their places will not be filled. But although I have not a single man too many to carry on the work, I do think I can reduce the staff.

The minister stated last year that the Surveys branch of his department was years ahead of settlement-I think he actually used those words. When the work is manifestly decreasing, according to the minister's own statement, and when very few new homesteads are being taken up, why should it be necesary to have an Assistant Director General of Surveys in that branch? There is ground there for criticism.

speechtext: I meant to answer the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). Mr. Shanks, whose appointment was discussed before dinner, has been in this service for twenty or twenty-two years and for a long time he has been drawing the same salary that he is getting to-day. Dr. Deville is becoming aged and somewhat infirm and Mr. Shanks has been assisting him. Surveyor General. Of course to the uninitiated these things are misleading and the statement my hon. friend holds in his mind is somewhat misleading. He doubtless was under the impression that this was an entirely new appointment, but such is not the case.

I gather that from what the minister has just said. If the Director General himself is now an old man, why not superannuate him and give Mr. Shanks the position?

That possibly will happen in due course. As the older men are superannuated these reductions will go on. I am grateful to the hon. member for South Oxford for the very kindly way he spoke about the staff. I agree with him thoroughly, but I do not want it to be inferred that I let my sympathies run away with my good judgment. On the other hand, I have some sympathy for the man who spends ten or fifteen years in the service; it is rather a serious thing for him to be pitchforked out into the world, because he is entirely uninitiated in business pursuits. In some cases we have to do that, but in the main we should use some judgment in the matter and try to make a transfer or other change that will obviate the necessity of taking that course.
