speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. We
do not pay rent.

You do not pay any rent
in your department?

Does the minister
question the correctness of Grattan O'Leary's figures which I quoted from MacLean's Magazine of February 1st? If so, in what respect are they incorrect?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to numbers and cost?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume
they are correct.
Will the minister give the details of the saving of $700,000 odd which he says has been effected in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I gave those details the other day. That is all on Hansard.
When the minister says he presumes that the figures given in MacLean's Magazine are correct he is admitting overmanning and is admitting increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, no, my hon. friend should not put words in my mouth. He knows there is the inside service at Ottawa, and the outside service is the civil government list and the list paid from the general 183
vote. One of the difficulties with respect to Mr. O'Leary's statement is that it is based only on the statement of the number of people employed at Ottawa. I have been . trying to get the Ottawa figures for my hon. friend, which I assume are the figures given by Mr. Grattan O'Leary. What are the figures for 1922 as given by him?

I will give my hon. friend the figures which I think he will be very much interested in. The figures to which he is now taking exception are:
Employees Salaries
1921	
1,238	$2,119,8181922	
1,324	2,402,6801923	(nine	months).. ..	1,329	1,794,488
In the case of the last item, at the rate for the nine months' period, the total for the year would be $2,512,648. Then there is the survey question with which I dealt at a good deal of length both last year and the year before, in the hope of bringing about some economies in connection with that service. I also urged we should try and have our estimates so prepared that the country would have a chance of knowing, and hon. members also, what the cost of running any particular department was. We do not know to-day. My hon. friend, I think, does not know today, because we have our employees tucked away in this, that and the other vote. I think my hon. friend will recollect the argument I made in connection with that matter. Now, admittedly there are far more employees in the Department of the Interior than is shown by the civil service list. There is no question about that and I think my hon. friend will agree with me. I had hoped that he might be able to make some headway in preparing the figures for presentation to the House in such a form that we would know where we are, would know what real economies, if any, are being made. But I point out to my hon. friend that these figures, to which he did not take exception but which he admitted to my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) were correct, show when these outside services are considered that there has not been any reduction but rather an increase in cost, and not only an increase in cost but also an increase in numbers. Now, perhaps, my hon. friend would give us the exact figures of all these employees at the present time. I think he will find that his offhand idea was not correct, and that the figures given are substantially right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply
to my hon. friend I would say that the figures I have here show a total in January, 1922,

Supply-Interior

of 1,325, and in January, 1924, of 1,300, or a net reduction of 25 in the Ottawa service. But in both the inside and outside services there is a reduction of 92.

With reference to
the explanation given by the minister as to what appears to be a new appointment, that is to say the Assistant Director General of Surveys, he stated that this gentleman had formerly been Assistant Surveyor General. I find that to be the case. In the estimates for 1924, and in those for 1922, I find there was an Assistant Surveyor General at a salary of 13,666 and the amount has been constantly increasing. I notice in the estimates now before the committee there appears an item of $4,140 for the salary of an Assistant Surveyor General, in addition to the salary for a new appointee as Assistant Director General of Surveys of $4,350. Does the minister wish the committee to understand that this appointee is drawing the salary of Assistant Surveyor General and also the salary of the new Assistant Director General of Surveys? The salary for the old position still appears in the estimates, it was there in 1922, and I presume it has been there for many years.
I repeat, that in the estimates we are considering there appears the salary of an Assistant Surveyor General $4,140 and in 1922 the amount appeared as $3,666. This gentleman is certainly receiving considerable attention from his friends if he is able to draw two salaries and has been receiving such a substantial increase all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not true; he is not drawing two salaries.

Then how does it
appear that the item still figures in the estimates, and that there is a salary for a new appointment as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will understand we are bringing men in ' from the outside and cutting down the outside staff. I can assure my hon. friend there is no increase. Mr. Shanks was appointed to assist the Director General of Surveys, more particularly and his classification is under that heading. We brought no new men into the service and do not propose to do so.

Did Mr. Shanks
occupy the position of Assistant Surveyor General?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
That still appears in the estimates. Who occupies that position at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no one in that position.
Why should it appear in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will have to give me an opportunity to readjust my department, which I am trying to do daily. I am not creating any new positions, and it is not the intention to increase that staff. This gentleman has been given that position, and the hon. member will notice that we are dropping a reclamation engineer further down the list, whose salary was $4,800. So that in dropping our reclamation and survey work we have to make all these changes and arrangements.

If there is any intention to make a reduction, surely this item should not appear in the estimates this year, the position being abolished. If the reduction the minister refers to has taken place, and the staff is being reduced, as has been stated, the Assistant Surveyor General is surely a new appointment. If a new position is being created and the old one is being maintained, and we are asked to vote the amount that has been in the estimates for years, there is no reduction.

The minister informed the committee this afternoon that he assumed no responsibility for salaries, and that that was a matter for the Civil Service Commission. I want to make it perfectly clear that I do not believe in reducing salaries. I believe that men are entitled to a fair and reasonable wage. I do not think that where the salaries are reasonable at the present time they should be reduced. But 'there is another phase of the matter which has to do with this item, and that is as to the question of over-staffing and overlapping. I presume the minister will assume responsibility for that, if there is any, and he would not try to put that off on the Civil Service Commission. What is he doing in that regard? What is he doing, along with the other ministers of the Crown, to endeavour to correct any overlapping or over-staffing? It may be that there are men in one department who are doing the same work, and it is not necessary to have more than one at that particular work. If that is so, and if the country is paying men for holding positions where they do not require to do a fair day's work, the minister should investigate and deal with such cases. I notice that some charges have been made by Mr. O'Leary in this connection. I will quote a short extract from MacLean's Magazine of March 1, this year, which reads:

Supply-Intenor
For an uprooting of waste from the Oivil Service can never be achieved by the mere indiscriminate dismissal of a few hundred civil servants. What is required is a major operation. What is needed is not so much a combing of branches as a sheer abolition of branches, a ruthless extinction of overlapping and duplication and of wasted, futile effort. Let me give an illustration of what I mean:
Two government departments carry establishments for precise levelling.
Three departments have establishments in connection with topographical maps.
Seven departments have photostat establishments.
Five departments support establishments and equipment for the purpose of blue printing and reproductions.
One department has five distinct engineering branches; and it is said that only one of these operates under the departmental engineer.
Dredging, with its costly overhead engineering establishments, is carried on in three different departments.
Surveying work is carried on in three different branches of one department.
One department has seven distinct branches dealing with lands, each having its own expensive overhead establishment.
Now the need here is not for dismissals; it is for wholesale abolition, or at least intelligent consolidation. Dismissal of a few hundred employees would mean a saving of some thousands of dollars; ordinary, common-sense centralization would mean a saving of millions.
Would the minister agree to the correctness of that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I
would like to say, however, that the gentleman must have known when he made the statement about the Land's department, or he should have known if he had made inquiry, that those several branches were moved into the Norlite building and amalgamated under one head at the time that article was written. As for the other accusations, I did not follow my hon. friend very carefully, I am speaking for my department. However, before that article was written, these changes were made along the line of reorganization and work which I have been endeavouring to carry on in the department. With a staff of 1,200 or 1,300 people the minister should be given a little time to effect economies and savings. I think I can point with a great deal of pride to having done so. I do not say that I am through. One difficulty is that there are a number of men on my staff who have given splendid service to the people of the country, and spent years of their lives at it. In due course they will have to be retired. I expect a number will be retired this year, and in fairness to them I do not wish to mention their names at the moment. I am endeavouring to effect economies. I cannot reduce the staff from 800 to a very large extent next year but I hope to reduce it in a considerable degree.
As for economies in the outside service, naturally our work is reduced. I think threequarters of a million, plus four hundred thousand, is a fairly decent showing. If my hon. friend thinks it is not, all I can say is that it is hopeless to attempt to make him realize the fact that one is trying at least to do his very level best to effect economy in a very large department. That is my feeling and I cannot help saying it.

I was chairman of the
Civil Service committee last year, and I think all the hon. members who took part in the investigation before that committee and in the recommendations to the government with reference to the superannuation scheme will agree with me that the very question which the hon. member fo"r New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) is discussing was paramount in the minds of the committee when dealing with this question. We hear criticism of the government when faithful employees are retired, and if any more of our employees were retired without superannuation we would hear still more criticism. The bill for superannuation has been referred to a committee and we hope that it will be passed this session. That bill will cover many eases to which the hon. member for New Westminster refers, it is going to give an opportunity for many faithful servants of the government for the past thirty-five years to retire to private life on a superannuation adequate to the service which they have given to the state, and I think all members on both sides of the House who criticise overmanning would be better to withhold their criticism until such time as the superannuation bill has been put into effect and the economy in connection with old employees has been adjusted according to the retirements under the Superannuation Act. The amalgamation of services will then be possible.

With regard to
withholding our criticism, I should like to ask the minister further in connection with what appears to be a new appointment on page 76 of the Estimates, because the fact that the Assistant Surveyor General is being transferred to another position does not justify having the two items appear in the estimates. There is still the old position of Assistant Surveyor General appearing on this page of the estimates, and there is a new appointment of Assistant Director General of Surveys. Why is it that the two salaries should appear in the estimates for the one official, because we are informed that this is merely a transfer from one position to the other? Surely one of them could be dropped if that is the case.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have explained to my hon. friend that we are in the reorganization stage all down the line. I have at the moment transferred under one head seven land branches at the head office. We were enabled to do that when we secured premises into which we could move our people, and make that saving by getting them all into one building. One of the difficulties in this city is that the department is housed in seventeen different buildings.

I am not surprised
at that judging from the leases that have been brought down recently.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was a condition of affairs that was in existence when I took office and it is still in existence. We happened to find ourselves in that position. Bringing these branches from buildings which were not contiguous before and placing them all in one building, we are able to put them under one head. That was known when that article was written, 'and while I have no quarrel with Grattan O'Leary over the articles he writes, my work is to make savings in the department where that is humanly possible. While I expect to make savings by reorganization, still I am not in a position to come into the House and abolish those positions in a moment. There is no one at the moment drawing a salary as Assistant Surveyor General. Mr. Shanks who occupied that position is drawing the salary of the other position.

Then, why not
strike it out of the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
In connection with the savings to which the minister refers, I have in my hand the estimates for the year

ended March 31, 1922, showing that this official who has been transferred to the new position of Assistant Director General of Surveys is receiving an increase in salary of $690. That does not indicate any great inclination on the part of the minister to curtail expenses in any way. At the same time knowing that he has been transferred from 'one position to another, the minister allows this item to appear in the estimates for the old position of Assistant Surveyor General at a salary of $4,140, and an item for the new position at a salary of $4,350. I do not think it is fair to the committee that we should be asked to ferret out these things. The minister ought to be frank with the committee and intimate what is being done rather than force us to the work of worming these things out of the minister as we have had to do time and again since this session has commenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have explained to my hon. friend over and over again what has been done in this particular case, but my hon. friend persists in misunderstanding me.

I do not persist in misunderstanding the minister at all. I beg to differ from the minister in that respect, and if the minister states what is correct, there is no justification for the two items appearing in the estimates and for asking us to pass them in this way. I will venture to state that this is unheard of and has never before occurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has been done every year, and my hon. friend who has been/ in this House for some years should know that that sort of thing has been done every year. You cannot on the 31st March abolish a position with an occupant whom you are not sure is going to be superannuated. The committee will have to take the word of the minister, as they always have to do, that this position Is not going to be filled beyond a certain time. Mr. Shanks had been promoted to be Assistant Director General of Surveys. The other position is not filled. I am asking the committee to give me an opportunity to reorganize and in some cases to reclassify and cut down this staff. I have pointed out the accomplishment as regards the Lands branch. I want to <io the same in this case. My hon. friend will persist in misunderstanding me or in assuming that I am trying to cover up something. I have been absolutely open about every item in connection with these estimates and I have been trying my level best to explain them.

Supply-Interior

The minister will recall that before six o'clock I asked whether any new appointments were being made in this branch of the service and I was informed that that was not the case. Apparently this is a new appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a new classification. It does not add to the personnel by a single individual. I trust my hon. friend will take my word for that.

We are asked to
vote an amount to pay the salary of a new official and we are asked also to vote an amount that was in the estimates of last year for the old position. The minister now informs the committee that it is not his intention to fill the old position. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then, why not
strike this out of the estimates and be done with it. so that we may know what we are doing.
The minister, on thinking this over, will see that he is taking somewhat of an impossible position. If this is a matter of reclassification, the old office goes. There is no dispute about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is quite true, but it may not be done on the particular date at which we vote it.

Let us get down to facts. If my hon. friend admits that this is a reclassification, the old office goes. I think my hon. friend on sober thought will agree with me that that is the case. The reason for holding it, therefore, is not a matter of reclassification. If it be not a matter of reclassification, but a matter of creating a new office, the previous position stands and a new office is created. My hon. friend will see that that is just what his vote is doing. It is either one thing or the other. It cannot' be both. We have the old office standing, and unless my hon. friend abolishes it he is in the position of having created a new situation at an increased salary while keeping open to be filled one that is already in existence. I want to be absolutely fair to the minister. There is just one consistent course for him to take; he can do one of two things, either to admit frankly that this is a new job which is found to be necessary in the department and which does not prevent him from keeping the old one, or to acknowledge that the matter is one of re-classification, and do away with the old position. It is a question for the minister to settle; but he cannot take both views; it is impossible for him to do so. I want to help the minister, who tells us that he does not want to appoint anyone to the old position. The best way in which we can help the minister to make 100 per cent in the economics in his office this year is to strike out that vote. After all the talk about economy in the Civil Service he should not object to that $4,000 being struck out; here we have a chance of helping the minister in a few minutes to add to the good work of the year by striking out this vote. Does not the minister want to be helped? Why should he not strike out the vote, unless it is that the job is being retained for someone else?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not.
Then why not strike out the vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I have
stated half a dozen times, I expect to be able to cut down the service-at least I am so informed by some 12 or 15 persons.
Is that all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By retirements at least; I do not say that is all. My hon. friend might as well say, why not wipe out all the salaries in connection with these positions? But we cannot do that.
I would not say that for one moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let me say that there is no desire to fill the position of Mr. Shanks; we do not need anyone to take it. And if it would obviate discussion at greater length I am prepared to cut it out. My hope however is that these 15 or 20 men will not draw salary beyond two oh three months; that is my expectation. But I am bound to ask for a vote to cover their salaries for the whole year. If it will facilitate matters I am ready to strike out the amount because Mr. Shanks has been established in his position. He was not so established when we prepared these estimates; he was in the same category as the others.
That is quite right, but such is no longer the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, for the reason I have stated; he has been established; but had it not been so we should have had to maintain the position.

The position the
minister takes is reasonable if he will adhere to it. This official seems to have been moved
Supply-Interior

up rapidly, and I might ask the minister at what age superannuation is obligatory. For some time past there has been a tendency to take back into the service people who have been superannuated and to pay them higher salaries than they previously received, the result being that on their final superannuation they have drawn a greater allowance, through their increased salary, than they would have been entitled to before. This official received an increase of $680 in the estimates of 1922. Is it possible that he is approaching the age of superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He has
seen 22 years of service. I do not know the man; I would not know him if I met him. The recommendations in regard to his service and his ability are splendid and I assume that they are correct; but I do not know, nor have I any personal interest in, Mr. Shanks.

How long will it
be before he is superannuated?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know.
Will he not be superannuated at a certain age?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He might be superannuated at any time owing to illness or from any other cause that might arise.
I understood there was a stated age.
The Calder Act fixes the age of compulsory superannuation at 70.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I move, Mr. Chairman,
that the item be reduced by $4,140.

Could we not
help the minister further? We have added to his batting average about 100 per cent. The minister has referred to various maps and all that sort of thing and he has been looking into the matter generally. But what is a cartographer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not prepared to define these classifications.
Is not a cartographer a man who works on maps?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Let me mention some of the details in connection with the great struggle which my hon. friend has been making against this avalanche of maps. Last year when we were discussing this subject we were told that- there was a number of people who were making maps. We had in this department 4 chief map draftsmen. Then
f Mr. S ut her la ud. 1
we had 11 principal map draftsmen; 26 senior map draftsmen; I senior relief map maker; 1 relief map maker; 12 map draftsmen; 1 junior map draftsman; 2 chief draftsmen; 4 senior draftsmen, 1 draftsman; 1 junior draftsman, and 4 cartographers. My hon. friend has been struggling with this problem and I want to compliment him on one thing: he has taken care to see that there are no more than 6 cartographers this year. The result of the minister's efforts has simply been this, that "what we have we hold." There is not one single; reduction made in this connection, although I thought that the discussion last year had at least shown that economies could be effected in regard to the number of persons we have engaged on maps. We have maps for everything; maps in this department and maps in that department; and we have surveys in this field and surveys in that field, an overlapping service here and the same there. We had this matter all discussed last year but my hon. friend has been unable to do anything. Now, can we help him to some extent? I say, there is not one single reduction effected; no attempt made to give effect to the protests of this overlapping and the like.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
no overlapping. I am sure my hon. friend must admit that there is none.
I do not know. These maps-I should think a good many of them by this time must be drawn one on top of the other. Does my hon. friend say he cannot effect any economies there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, not a
thing.

Mr. Chairman,
it is just as well that we should grasp where this is leading to. There is a little economy made here of $4,000 in connection with the total of this vote as the result of all the work my hon. friend is-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course,
there is no credit for the three-quarters of a million dollars saved.

Three-quarters
of a million dollars saved! As my hon. friend knows full well, that saving is due to the curtailment of service to the public. I am not talking about the withdrawal of public conveniences, I am talking about the cost of service to the public, notwithstanding the withdrawal of the conveniences.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Will my
hon. friend name one convenience which has been withdrawn from the public?

Supply-Interior

My hon. friend knows-and I am not blaming him for doing it; it is the right thing to do-that he has closed offices which were open for the purpose of convenience to the public in certain localities. As I say, I am not blaming him for closing those offices-
Oh, oh.

I am not blaming him for closing them, but the economy which is effected, as my hon. friend knows who laughs, is by reason of the curtailment of this service. I am talking about the cost of the reduced service to the public, and as admitted by the minister-I do not know that the hon. gentleman who laughs was in the House at the time-the net reduction in connection with this particular vote comes down to some four thousand odd dollars. It is true we have added 100 per cent to it by striking out an amount of $4,100. But that is the net result of all this work. Now we have services here and services there, employees inside and employees outside, employees that are shown on this list and hundreds of employees that are not shown, and we have an approximate cost in 1921 of $2,119,000 odd, in 1922 of $2,400,000 odd and in 1923 of $2,500,000 odd.
Will the hon. gentleman read the figures between 1911 and 1921? He will find a real increase there.

I am just
dealing with the figures I have before me.

You have those figures
before you there also.

I have not. But does the hon. member think that what was done some other year has anything to do with the necessity for economy in this particular year? Is that his idea of the duty of a public servant?

But you had control
in those years.
What difference does that make? Supposing that what was done was wrong-and I am going to tell my hon. friend, as the fact is, that the votes for those years were considerably less than in 1922-

And the rate of pay
much higher to-day.

The votes are
a great deal less, and the numbers are less.
If my hon. friend wants to debate it we will debate it. I take the year 1921 with a vote of $2,100,000, the year 1922, for which my hon. friend's government is responsible-
No, no.
All right, I will take some other year that you are interested in. I will take the vote of 1923 amounting to $2,500,000.

Covered by statutory
increases.

This is a
wonderful economy 1 It is an economy which is costing more and more and more in service all the time.
No.

Yes; with less
facilities to the public. But if the hon. minister says he cannot do anything better I am not going to delay the vote. It is perfectly ridiculous to talk of economy in the face of those figures, as every hon. gentleman knows.

Did I understand the
minister to say that he did not know anything about the leases of the premises occupied by his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No,, the
leasing is in charge of the Public Works department.

It seems to me that we are finding out a great many things in the department which the minister does not know anything about. We have found out now that he does not know anything about the leases of the premises occupied by his department. He told us some time ago that he did not know anything about the salaries in his department; he did not know anything about the salary revision in his department; he did not know that the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, which includes employees in his department, were asking for salary revision; he did not know the number of employees in his department; he did not know the amount that his department is costing for salaries. Now, it seems to me this is a business proposition and that he as the head of this department ought to obtain this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let me say to my hon. friend that if he is asking for real information he will get it; if he is not, I want seriously to protest against his endeavour to create the impression that the minister does not know anything about his department.

I did not say that.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
You did say so.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It meant
practically the same thing. That is the impression which my hon. friend wants to create, and I think we have come to the point where patience ceases to be a virtue. I have endeavoured to be fair and to give all the information I possibly could. Then to be told that the minister does not know anything about his department convinces me that there are some courtesies at least due to a poor minister who happens to be so unfortunate as to have to answer a thousand and one questions that have no relevance to the estimates whatever. I am quite prepared to answer any legitimate questions.
Mr. Chairman, I did not say or suggest that the minister did not know anything about his department at all. Perhaps there are some things he knows about
Read Hansard to-morrow, and you will find you did say so.

I did not say anything of the kind, but I did mention certain things that admittedly the minister does not know anything about,-things which, I think he should know something about. To get down to business, take the matter of leases. I do not see any occasion for the minister to get excited about this.

Mr. Chairman,
may I interrupt? Surely the hon. member is out of order. We are discussing civil government. The matter of leases comes under my department.
Yes, the hon. member is out of order, this resolution being for salaries and contingencies of the Department of the Interior.

All right, I have to accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, if you do not want to hear anything about leases. It seems to me that certainly the minister should know something about the leases of the premises which his department occupies here in Ottawa.

have to be furnished for the expenditure.

speechtext: We do if they are travelling outside of Canada.
But in Canada? I understand that in certain of the provinces that change has lately been made and they find that a great saving has been effected.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

The amount being asked for is a re-vote, parliament having voted $30,000 last year. Have we been
given all the papers m regard to the Belle River matter?
Mr. KING (Kootenay) [DOT] Yes

The file stops
apparently in 1922. The top letter is dated December 30, 1922. Is that the last of the list, or are the letters not in order?
I think that is the beginning of the file.

Taking the
year 1922, can the minister tell me what work had been undertaken by the government as at January 1922 at Belle River?

There was no
work in 1922. My record shows the last expenditure to have been made in 1921, until last year.
What was done in 1921?

There was $400
for dredging.
To what depth was that dredging done in 1921 and for what purpose?

relieve shoaling in the channel; it was to clear the channel.

Dredging of
course is always done to clear something; at least it is supposed to, although it does not do so always. Will the minister give us some more definite information? What depth was dredged or supposed to be dredged in 1921?

I have not that
information in my notes, and it is not usual to expect a question of that kind. I was asked when last we were in committee to ascertain the amount of the expenditure year by year. What work is contemplated at this point? This is merely the commencement of the operations which the department evidently has in view. The return brought down clearly indicates that the building of a pier on one side of the river will have to be duplicated by a pier on the other side; and at present there is apparently no necessity for this work so far as can be seen by those who are familiar with the location. Evidently there is a company which is anxious that something should be done in the way of establishing a port at this point. I think the correspondence which has been

Supply-Public Works
brought down, although I have not had an opportunity recently of looking into it in detail, shows that an expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars is contemplated in this connection. There certainly is no pressing need for any such expenditure at this point just now, as those who are familiar with the situation at Belle River realize. This is a case of political expediency rather than of real necessity on the part of the department and it is quite apparent from the return which has been brought down at this session that it is not contemplated to let the matter end here; it is anticipated that nearly $200,000, according to the statement of an official of the department, will be necessary to make this port of any use. And even at that it is to be a pleasure resort for the recreation at Belle river of people coming across from Detroit. There is absolutely no need of an expenditure of this kind at the present time, and the necessity for curtailing expenses in every direction in this country is so imperious to-day that the minister would be well advised to eliminate this item from the estimates.

Would you not
pay the contractor who has completed the work under the vote of last year?

The minister understands that the vote was put through last year under rather peculiar circumstances such as would hardly justify it. I am not aware of the nature of the contract which has been let, and I am merely pointing out that there is absolutely no necessity for an expenditure of this kind at this particular point under present conditions. This is an expenditure that might well be deferred for years to come; it will be a long time before anything of this character can be contemplated with justification. When the matter was first approached by the then Minister of Railways who represented the constituency it was clearly shown by the officials of the department that something in the neighbourhood of $200,000 would be necessary before any useful purpose could be served. The Northern Navigation Company .are really the ones who are anxious to have this made a port of landing for their boats to look after the tourist traffic between Detroit and this point. I think my hon.
friend was not in the House on the last occasion when we discussed this matter-

-because the whole history of the contract and the necessity for the work was gone into very thoroughly and my hon. friends were informed that we were asking a revote to pay for construction that was done on a vote passed by this House last year. The amount of the contract is $27,663.26. This money has been earned by the contractor. As to the necessity for the work, I think very good evidence has been furnished to the committee. During the war years the department continued to spend money at this point, and surely they were not spending it unnecessarily at that time. The harbour at Belle River is an old settled community, I am informed, and probably it has been unfairly treated in this House. My hon. friend speaks of this being a political vote, but I do not look upon it as such at all. A large amount of lumber and beet shipments, amounting to 1,350 tons, were handled there last year. I believe this waterway is necessary in order that the people may carry on. We hear a great deal about Canadians being attracted to the other side of the line. I am told that just opposite Belle River on the American side there are proper harbour facilities, and the officials of my department inform me that this work is necessary for the people at Belle River. It is true that we have gone further than has been the policy of the department in the past. It is hoped that by building this retaining wall we will prevent the silting up of the channel and so avoid the dredging which has been necessary year after year. The larger scheme my hon. friend refers to has been reported upon by the engineer, but not accepted by the department. It would give greater security and improve the harbour facilities, but is beyond what we think is necessary at the present time. We are simply asking for a revote to pay for the work authorized by this parliament last year.

Does the work
contemplate the building of a pier on each side of the river?

No, just on one
side.

It has been already
pointed out by the engineering officials of the department that it would be absolutely useless to build1 a pier on one side of the river without also building a parallel pier on the other side to prevent the filling up of the channel.

The engineering
officials have not made any such statement.
Supply-Public Works

They have suggested that the building of a retaining wall on the other side would help very materially to relieve what we are trying to overcome, but at the present time this is all the work we expect to do, and we believe it will be a benefit to the community.
What river is this harbour on?
I have no doubt that my hon. friend knows the local geography much better than I do. I am assuming that Belle river is the river that this harbour is on. Am I right?
No.

I do not know
the country. I shall be glad to have my hon. friend inform me.

As I do not know of

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

I expect he would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
always glad to accommodate my friend from South Oxford, we have been in public life a good many years together, but always looking at each other from different angles. Belle River is Belle River; it is not the Thames river or any other river.
All the worse for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is one of the nicest little towns located in one of the nicest spots in western Ontario.
River or town?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The river is composed of water and the town is composed of land and houses; you can hardly compare them. But the country, as hon. gentlemen who travel through that part of Ontario know, is very flat and one of the chief items of expenditure is drainage. Now, Belle River is a town situated on what is known as Belle river. I have never heard it called anything else, and I have travelled through there a good many times. This matter was first brought to my attention by the late Minister of Railways, Mr. Kennedy, who, as eveiybody in this House knew, was not given to doing things that were not necessaiy and who was not much of a man to be asking for grants for his own constituency. This was brought to my attention in the first place shortly after he was elected. There are several reasons why this little harbour should be enlarged. One is because there is a lot of business capable of being done at Belle River. The population there is anxious to get its coal in by boat, to start with, and it cannot do so under present circumstances. I am talking perhaps against railway interest, when I say this, but I am talking on behalf of the people. There is a prosperous farm population in that vicinity and they are devoting their attention more and more to sugar beet production. There is the export movement of sugar beets, probably via the river Thames, and besides, one or two of the sugar beet refineries have to, import a certain quantity of sugar beets annually in order to make up their requirements. If there is any section in Canada that is entitled to some development on account of the necessities of the situation, it is Belle River. I know that a good deal of fun has been poked at it, and there is the suggestion that there never was a Belle river proper. I do not blame hon. gentlemen for taking full advan-

Supply-Public Works
tage of the situation and offering criticism, but I have been there many times and I know the conditions. This money was voted by parliament; the contractor has done his work and wants his pay. The vote is to provide for that payment for work done by the contractor according to the orders of parliament through the Public Works department.

I have a letter in my hand
written by an inhabitant of Belle River. He speaks about the mouth of the river being filled up with the drifting silt, so I have no doubt it is a river-"the Belle river"-he says I do not think it is necessary to read the letter; it is much along the line of what the Minister of Railways has just said.

It is a joke to call it a river. It is a low, flat tract of land, and if you are going to keep it open you will be constantly dredging it. So far as the sugar beet industry is concerned, the exchange of sugar beets between the United States and Canada is in the other direction. The beets are being shipped to Michigan and not through this port at all. They are loaded on the cars and shipped from the eastern part of the county of Lambton.

I think it was
$400 that was spent at this place in 1921. Will the minister give me the other figures that he relies upon in justification for his position-the amounts spent in other years?

I do not know
that we can very well lock the door after the horse has been stolen, but the horse was stolen all right. Yes, and we did our best to stop it. We had the bill here; we had everything here. We heard all about Tim needing [DOT] King and King needing Tim. We heard of the price that was paid.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend says, "Oh, no," but everything was produced here, and there was no question about it. There was no question where Mr. Cooper was in that election. There was no question who got those dodgers out; there was no question as to whom those dodgers were used for. Of course the price was paid. I do not know that we can do anything now except again enter our protest that elections are carried on in such a way without something being done through the criminal courts.
There was the admitted bill; there was the admitted deal. There was the consideration to be given, and the government endorses the cheque. How much of this vote is to be paid the present contractor?
Then why should not the vote be put in at that amount?

There are always contingencies, engineering ex-
11 p.m. penses, and so on to make up the balance. That is the contractor's fee; as my hon. friend knows there are other items.
I do not know at all. Will any part of this vote be used for extra work that the country is not now liable for?

No, the work is
complete now.

What is the character
of the work that has been done? Is there a wharf, and if so, what is the size of it? What dredging has been done?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:

the hon. member (Sir Henry Drayton) may be put right, that this work was asked for when the late Minister of Railways was still in the full vigour of health, and the work would have been done had that by-election never taken place.

These things
sometimes chime in, but whether they do or not there is no question as to the corrupt offer made to that electorate. In reply to the

speechtext:

Chatham-repairs to the revetment wall, $4,000.

This amount of
$4,000 is required to complete the contract entered into with William Bermingham for the renewal of 182 lineal feet of the revets ment wall at McGregor's Creek. Here are the details of the estimated cost:

 5,098 00

184*
In regard to extras the district engineer reports that when the contractor commenced to drive piles he found it impossible to penetrate the hard material without iron shoes on each pile which were provided for in the tender form, and even with shoes it was impossible to reach rock, which was called for under the specifications of the contract. The extra cost of using iron shoes was $6 per pile or a total of $366 and the contractor was authorized to proceed with the driving using shoes. In addition to this the contractor wishes to be reimbursed for the extra length of piles over and above what he actually finds possible to place in the work. The district engineer, Mr. Craig, states that assuming they are able to get 35 feet of penetration the extra length will amount to approximately 12 feet per pile or about $732. It was also found that the old material did not make sufficient backfill as it was not porous enough to allow sufficient run off of any underground water. The contractor was therefore authorized to secure and place in the work 150 cubic yards of coarse sand and gravel at 75 cents per cubic yard. Then as to the extension of the contract the explanation is rather long but I will read it if the committee wishes. The section up there is a rather difficult one and a certain amount of work had to be put in which the engineer thought would be sufficient and would withstand pressure. He found, however, that there had been a slip back of the wall, that there had been a movement, and it was necessary to reinforce and strengthen the wall which cost an additional amount of $3,200. If the committee would like further explanation I would not object to reading the engineer's report.
Dispense.

I have given a
brief statement of what the report contains.

My hon. friend's hearing apparently is not very good.

I did not catch
the observation.

I think I can
save my hon. friend's voice. I do not think he need read the report, it is probably wrong and we will let it go at that.
Supply-Public Works

Before the item carries I
would like to ask a question. I have asked it before but I have never been Ale to get a satisfactory answer. Here is a small item of $4,000. Now, I understand that under the British North America Act certain matters have been allotted to the Dominion government and other matters to the provincial authorities. Can the minister explain-we have the Minister of Railways here, he is an old parliamentarian-why it is that such small undertakings as these devolve upon the Dominion government whereas other works such as the building of elevators, and the construction of creameries, which cost twice as much, are left to the provincial governments. I suppose there is a good reason for it but I should like to have it explained. Then I could feel more like voting for such enterprises as these. What is ithe fundamental authority for spending this money?

The Dominion
government own property in that vicinity and this revetment or retaining wall was filled in for the protection of that property.
Does that apply in every case where money is spent for these wharves?
This is a retaining wall to prevent property slipping in. It is built to retain the earth in position.

That is not what I am
trying to get at. Surely in all those cases the work is not on property owned by the Dominion government. In every little fishing village if it seems to be right that there should be a wharf or harbour built, the Dominion government undertakes to build it.

Yes. Under the
British North America Act the government assumes that responsibility.

I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) wants to get definite information on that question. As I understand it, the question does not depend at all upon either the amount or the importance of the undertaking. It has rather to do with the sub-division of governmental activities in this country. There is no duty at all, as the hon. gentleman will see, thrown upon the provinces to look after our harbours and rivers. Just in the same wTay there is no duty thrown upon the Dominion to look after the courthouses of the provinces. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Cobourg-reconstruction of harbour works and dredging, $50,000.

How does that
work stand?

The $24,200 is a re-vote this year. It requires $20,000 to complete the contract. Y. T. Bartram is the contractor. The items are as follows:
To complete contract with V. T. Bartram for the reconstruction in concrete of 170 lineal feet of the superstructure of the east pier immediately south of the lighthouse, width of work 30 feet, $20,000.
Dredging, cleaning up inner and outer harbours to depth of 20 feet, ($4,225 of this to complete contract No. 14,320 with Frontenac Dredging Company), $30,479.50. Total amount required, $50,497.50. Say $50,000.

Let us get this a little more clearly in our heads. We start with a contract of $25,000, because I assume the government will hold that contract within the vote. What is the initial contract under the vote of 1923-24?

The initial contract was $18,222. That is the contract for the concrete superstructure of the east pier. Then $20,000 is asked to cover not only the contract, but inspection and other fees. Then there is the dredging and cleaning up of the inner and outer harbours to a depth of twenty feet, $30,497. We are asking for $50,000.

When was the
later contract let?
The 14th of September, 1923.

What was the
authority for it?

An order in
council.
Where was the vote?

We had a vote
last year.

That was $25,000 and at the time apparently the department let a second contract. I do not know if my hon. friend is right, but I hope he is wrong. Out of a total vote which gives them the right to commit this country to a given expenditure of $25,000 they increase the liability to $48,497.
Yes.

I think the minister is wrong. Suppose he tries again.

Supply-Public Works

No, I am not
wrong. We let a contract for the superstructure of the east pier for $18,222, that is a contract for breakwater reconstruction and also a contract for some dredging which was to be completed under this arrangement this year. We are asking for a vote of $50,000, of which $30,000 will be for dredging.
In the fiscal year 1923-24 a vote was passed in the House for $25,000. During the recess we have had two contracts let on the authority of that vote of $25,000.
No.
What was the authority?
The contract was let on the general dredging vote.

The minister
did not tell me that at first. There is just one thing done in connection with that which was wrong.

I do not think
so.

If the minister
thought it was wrong he would not say so anyway. He would not come to the House and say he had brought in something which was improper. I would not expect him to be quite so silly as to admit it and I do not ask his admission. But I am pointing out that it is not good practice to cover specific contracts under your general vote for dredging; and then afterwards, to greatly increase your rights under your general vote by a large revote this year which you try to justify as being a vote to carry out e contract which was entered into to be paid out of the general vote although the general vote was never put to that purpose.

No that is not
correct.

It has not been put to that purpose. There is no use in my hon. friend shaking his head. If it had been put to that purpose this vote would not be here. I am not saying this has not been done lots of times.

We contract
under the general vote right along and now we come before parliament this year, the vote having expired, and we put in a special item.
How many more contracts are there in this list which are justified under the general vote?

We have the
item for dredging. I have not the information which my hon. friend asks for with me.

The amount of the vote ought to be known and the amount of the contracts made under it ought to be known before any specific contracts are considered in connection with it. I am going to ask my hon. friend when he can give me that information, if he cannot give it now.

The proper time to give it is now when we are considering contracts which are let under the general vote. I do not think the minister has understood the point. I am not questioning the amount of money which is being [DOT] spent under that vote; I am questioning the advisability of continuing a vote which allows work to be commenced impossible of being finished within the term of the vote. In other words, the real function of the general vote, I certainly would have thought, would be to look after general dredging to be done through the provinces apart from the consideration of some specific contracts by parliament. I do not suppose there is any doubt about that. If there is, will my hon. friend tell me?
There is no doubt at all.
That is to enable work to be done apart from special votes for specific contracts by parliament. Is that right?
Go ahead.

The minister will see, if he will just go a step further, that if that be the object of the vote, it is quite another thing to turn around and make that vote the justification for entering into contracts not to be performed under the general vote, but to be made the purpose of a specific vote and committing the House to that specific vote, because, it is said, a contract has already been entered into under the general vote.
Supply-Public Works
I think my hon. friend misunderstands me. A contract was entered into last year with the Frontenac Dredging Company to be paid out of the general vote.

This sets the

The minister

Yes.

Prior-?
[Sir Henry Drayton. J

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

What is the
object of purchasing a wharf at Jackson's Point, and from whom is it being purchased?

The proposed
amount of $6,500 is required to provide for expropriation and for the reconstruction of timber crib work of wharf 159 feet long by 36 feet wide, including warehouse and right of way, notice of expropriation having been filed in January 1924. The cost of reconstruction is $2,100. There was an expenditure under the vote of last year of $2,047.
But why is the property being bought?

It is quite a
long story. There are letters from the Jackson's Point Board of Trade and resolutions from the council of the Chippewa Band, Georgian island, from the council of the township of King and others.
Is there no government wharf there at all?
I think not.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Jeannette's Creek-wharf repairs, $1,000.

Where is Jeannette's
Greek?
In Kent county. This expenditure is for anchor piles and tie rods for the front wall of the wharf.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Kincardine-wharf repairs and reconstruction, $20,000.

Will the minister give
us particulars of this?

This is to continue reconstruction of the piling and wharfage along the western and south sides of the turning basin commenced in 1922. It is proposed to reconstruct the second section of 975 lineal feet with a concrete superstructure, leaving one more section to be completed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Leamington-repairs to pier, $1,000.
With what portion of these public works does the minister desire to conclude?
I should like to run through Ontario, if that would suit my hon. friend.

I suppose he
thinks he will have done a pretty good day's work if he gets that through?
Yes.

I have read
through this list pretty carefully, I think it is all right.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: LIQUOR AND NARCOTICS . TREATY WITH THE UNITED STATES FOR SUPPRESSION OF ILLICIT TRAFFIC

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: LIQUOR AND NARCOTICS . TREATY WITH THE UNITED STATES FOR SUPPRESSION OF ILLICIT TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Before the House adjourns, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention that at noon to-day the Secretary of State, for the government of the United States, and the Hon. Ernest Lapointe K.C., Minister of Justice of the Dominion of Canada, for the Canadian government signed a convention for the suppression of smuggling

Liquor and Narcotics
operations across the International boundary, the prosecution of persons violating the narcotic laws of either government, and for kindred purposes. Each government is to furnish information on request to the appropriate officers of the other concerning clearances of vessels or the transportation of cargoes, shipments or loads of articles across the International boundary, when the importation of the articles transported by land is subject to the payment of duties, also information respecting clearances of vessels to any ports when there is ground to suspect that the owners or persons in possession of the cargo intend to smuggle it into American or Canadian territory. Clearances are to be denied to vessels carrying cargo consisting of articles the importation of which is forbidden by either country when it is evident from the tonnage, size or general character of the vessel, or the length of the voyage, or certain other conditions that the vessel will be unable to carry the cargo to the destination proposed in the application for clearance. Arrangement is made for the return under reasonable conditions of stolen property brought into either country from the territory of the other when the owners are nationals of such other country. There is agreement that both countries shall exchange information concerning the names and activities of persons known to be engaged in the violation of the narcotic laws of the two countries. The convention also provides for the attendance of government officials of one country as witnesses in the other and the production of records and files or certified copies thereof in the trial of civil and criminal cases. Arrangement is made for the payment of cost of transcript of records depositions, certificates, letters rogotary, and the attendance of witnesses. Offences against the narcotic laws of the respective governments are added to the list of offences in the treaty now existing between the United States and Great Britain of May 18, 1908, with reference to reciprocal rights for the United States and Canada in the matters of conveyance of prisoners and wreckage and salvage, no penalty of forfeiture under the laws of the United States to be applicable or attach to alcoholic liquors or vessels, vehicles of persons by reason of the carriage in transit under Canadian guard through the territorial waters of the United States to Skagway, Alaska, and thence by the shortest route upwards of twenty miles to Canadian territory. Such transit is to be as now provided by law with respect to alcoholic liquors through the Panama canal or on the Panama railroad provided such liquors shall be kept
under seal continuously while they are carried within American territory and that no part of such liquors shall be at any time unladen therein. The convention is to take effect ten days from the date of the exchange of ratifications and to remain in force for one year and thereafter is terminable on thirty days' notice.
At the opening of the next sitting I will place on the Table a copy of the treaty which has been signed to-day.

speakerposition: topic
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On Monday
we propose to take up the estimates of the Department of External Affairs and matters relating to external affairs, such for example as the appropriation for the League of Nations, and also any matters incidental to the department, the Privy Council and the Governor General's office, and if time permits, we will return to estimates of the Public Works department.
Does that go as far as taking up the general question, having regard, for example, to the treaty with Turkey -or rather the lack of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Lausanne treaty, I presume, will be one of the main subjects of discussion.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Monday, June 9, 1924.
